◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tableau is a family of products, not just one. Knowing which tool to reach for in which situation is foundational. The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam tests product knowledge directly.

The Tableau product family

ProductPurpose
Tableau DesktopAuthoring tool; build workbooks, dashboards (paid)
Tableau PublicFree version of Desktop; saves to public cloud only
Tableau ServerOn-premises sharing platform
Tableau CloudCloud-hosted version of Server (Tableau Online rebrand)
Tableau Prep BuilderVisual data preparation tool
Tableau Prep ConductorServer add-on; schedule Prep flows
Tableau ReaderFree; view (not edit) .twbx workbooks locally
Tableau MobileiOS / Android apps for viewing
Tableau Embedded AnalyticsEmbed Tableau in custom apps

Licenses (creator / explorer / viewer)

Tableau uses ROLE-BASED licensing in Server/Cloud:

Creator
 Full authoring rights (Desktop + web authoring)
 Manage data connections, schedules
 Highest tier; ~$70/user/month (varies)

Explorer
 Edit existing workbooks in browser
 Create new dashboards from published data sources
 Cannot connect new data sources
 Mid-tier; ~$35-42/user/month

Viewer
 View-only access; interact with filters
 Can subscribe to alerts and emails
 Lowest tier; ~$12-15/user/month

Compare to Power BI's per-user vs per-capacity:
 Tableau is per-user with role-based pricing
 No "free for everyone" tier like Power BI Premium Capacity

File types

ExtensionContainsUse case
.twbWorkbook (XML); references to data sources, NO dataSmaller files; require source access
.twbxPackaged workbook: .twb + extracts + assetsSelf-contained; can email / archive
.tdsData source: connection + calculated fields, no dataShare connection setup
.tdsxPackaged data source: .tds + extractShare connection with data
.hyperExtract file (Hyper engine; newer)Performance-optimized data extract
.tdeOlder extract format (pre-2018.3)Legacy; auto-upgrades to .hyper
.tfl / .tflxTableau Prep flow / packaged flowPrep transformations
.tbmSaved bookmark (specific sheet view)Per-user saved view

Workbook structure

A workbook contains:

 Data sources — connections to your data
 Sheets — individual visualizations (one chart each)
 Dashboards — collections of sheets arranged together
 Stories — sequences of dashboards/sheets with narrative

Hierarchy:
 Workbook (.twb / .twbx)
 └─ Data Source(s)
 └─ Sheet 1, Sheet 2, ... (each is one viz)
 └─ Dashboard 1, Dashboard 2 (combine sheets)
 └─ Story 1, Story 2 (narrate dashboards)

Bottom of workbook UI:
 Tabs for each sheet/dashboard/story
 Color-coded icons distinguish types
 Click + buttons to create new of each type

Tableau Desktop vs Tableau Public

FeatureDesktop (paid)Public (free)
Save locally✓✗ (only to Tableau Public cloud)
PrivacyWorkbooks privateAll workbooks publicly visible
Data connectors100+ including DB, cloud, API~20 (files, Google Sheets, basic)
Data limitNo limit~15M rows per workbook
Extract refreshManual or scheduled (Server)Manual only
Best forCommercial; sensitive dataLearning, portfolio, blog vizzes

Tableau Server vs Cloud

Tableau Server (on-premises):
 Install on your own infrastructure
 Full control over security, performance, customization
 Hardware sizing requirements
 IT manages updates and backups
 Best for: large enterprises with strict data residency

Tableau Cloud (SaaS):
 Salesforce-hosted; previously called Tableau Online
 No infrastructure to maintain
 Auto-updates from Tableau
 Quicker to spin up; subscription-based
 Best for: most organizations now

Both support:
 - Publish workbooks
 - Schedule extract refreshes
 - Subscriptions and alerts
 - Permissions and projects
 - User management

Cloud has gradually become Tableau's default recommendation
Server still relevant for compliance / on-prem-only orgs

Versioning and compatibility

Tableau versions: YYYY.N format
 e.g., 2024.1, 2024.2, 2024.3 (three major releases per year)

Backward compatibility:
 Workbooks open in NEWER versions of Tableau
 Workbooks DON'T open in OLDER versions (without "save as previous version")

Save as previous version:
 File → Export As Version → choose older version
 Some features may not be preserved

Server/Cloud version >= Desktop version typically
 Otherwise: "workbook saved in newer version" error

Tableau release notes:
 Check what's new each version
 Common additions: new chart types, connectors, viz features
 E.g., 2020.2 introduced Relationships (now default over Joins)
 E.g., 2018.3 introduced Hyper extracts (.hyper)

Common version-specific features to know

Recent features (post-2020):
 - RELATIONSHIPS (logical layer; vs older Joins)
 - SET ACTIONS (allow user to drive sets via clicks)
 - Hyper extract format (replaces .tde)
 - Viz in Tooltip (mini-chart in tooltip)
 - Tableau Catalog (in Data Management add-on)
 - Tableau Prep Conductor (scheduled Prep flows)
 - In-product analytics (Explain Data, Ask Data)

Recent UI changes:
 - "Show Me" panel (was new in 2015; standard now)
 - "Data Source" tab at bottom
 - Improved web authoring

Stay current via Tableau Conference (annual) and release notes

Common ecosystem mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Confusing .twb and .twbx — .twb references data; .twbx packages it
  2. Using Tableau Public for confidential data — everything is public!
  3. Saving in newer version then trying to open in older — fails
  4. Buying Tableau Server when Tableau Cloud would do — unnecessary infrastructure
  5. Buying Creator licenses for everyone — Viewers cost much less
  6. Mixing Tableau and Tableau Prep workflows — Prep for ETL, Tableau for analysis
  7. Editing in Reader — Reader is view-only
  8. Forgetting that Tableau Public limits at 15M rows
  9. Treating .hyper and .tde as interchangeable — .hyper is newer (2018.3+) and preferred
★ ON THE EXAM

"Free version?" → Tableau Public (saves to public cloud).

"Build dashboards?" → Tableau Desktop.

"Share with team?" → Tableau Server or Tableau Cloud.

"Data prep tool?" → Tableau Prep Builder.

"Schedule Prep flows?" → Tableau Prep Conductor (Server add-on).

"View-only free?" → Tableau Reader.

"License tiers?" → Creator, Explorer, Viewer.

".twb vs .twbx?" → .twb is workbook only; .twbx packages data inside.

".hyper vs .tde?" → .hyper is newer (2018.3+); .tde is older/legacy.

"Workbook in older Tableau?" → Use File → Export As Version.

"Cloud vs Server?" → Cloud is SaaS; Server is on-prem.

"Server is now called?" → Tableau Server (still); Online became Tableau Cloud.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Tableau Desktop is the paid authoring tool; Tableau Public is the free version (saves to public cloud)
  • Tableau Server is on-premises sharing; Tableau Cloud is SaaS (formerly Tableau Online)
  • Tableau Prep Builder is for visual ETL; Conductor schedules Prep flows in Server
  • Tableau Reader is free, view-only
  • License roles: Creator (full), Explorer (edit), Viewer (view-only)
  • .twb = workbook only; .twbx = packaged with data and assets
  • .tds = data source only; .tdsx = packaged with extract
  • .hyper is the modern extract format (since 2018.3); .tde is legacy
  • Workbooks open forward (in newer versions) but not backward (without explicit Save as Version)
  • A workbook contains data sources, sheets, dashboards, and stories
  • Three major releases per year follow YYYY.N versioning
  • Relationships (logical layer) introduced in 2020.2 — now the default join model
  • Tableau Public limits at ~15M rows per workbook
  • Tableau Public is publicly visible — never use for confidential data
  • Most new orgs choose Tableau Cloud over Server for lower maintenance

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

You can't be productive in Tableau without knowing where everything lives. The interface is unique — drag-and-drop driven, with specific shelves and cards. The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam tests recognizing every part of the workspace.

The Tableau workspace tour

When you open a workbook, you'll see:

 Top: Menu bar (File, Data, Worksheet, Dashboard, Story, Analysis, Map, Format, Server, Window, Help)
 Top: Toolbar (Save, Open, New worksheet, Undo, Redo, Clear, Swap, Sort, Group, Highlight, Fit, etc.)
 
 Left side: Data pane and Analytics pane (toggle via tabs at top)
 Middle: Rows shelf, Columns shelf, Filters shelf, Marks card, Pages shelf
 Right: the actual viz canvas (where your chart appears)
 Bottom: Sheet tabs (worksheet / dashboard / story icons)
 Bottom: Data source tab (icon at far left)
 Far right (sometimes): Show Me panel

The Data pane (left side)

Lists all fields from the connected data source(s)

DIMENSIONS (above the dividing line; blue icons):
 Categorical or qualitative data
 Discrete by default
 Names, dates (some), region, product, etc.
 Drag to shelves to break the viz into categories

MEASURES (below the dividing line; green icons):
 Numerical / quantitative data
 Continuous by default
 Sales, profit, count of customers
 Drag to shelves to aggregate (default: SUM)

Tableau auto-classifies on first connect; you can move fields between categories
 Right-click field → Convert to Dimension / Measure

Field icons

IconMeaning
Abc (blue)String dimension
# (blue)Number (discrete dimension)
# (green)Number (continuous measure)
📅 (blue/green)Date dimension (discrete) or continuous date
🌍Geographic field (city, state, country, etc.)
T/FBoolean field
= (with prefix)Calculated field
{} (set)Set or group

The same field can appear discrete (blue pill) or continuous (green pill) on shelves depending on usage.

Shelves and cards

COLUMNS shelf
 Fields here define horizontal axis (x-axis)
 Discrete fields: each value becomes a column header
 Continuous fields: become a continuous axis

ROWS shelf
 Fields here define vertical axis (y-axis)
 Same rules as Columns

FILTERS shelf
 Fields here filter the data shown in the viz
 Right-click → Show Filter to expose as interactive control

PAGES shelf
 Field here creates an animation (one page per value)
 Useful for time-based animations

MARKS CARD
 Controls how marks (points, bars, lines) look:
 Mark type dropdown: Automatic, Bar, Line, Area, Square, Circle, Shape, Text, Map, Pie, Gantt, Polygon, Density
 Color — color encoding
 Size — size encoding
 Label — text on marks
 Detail — disaggregate to row level without showing
 Tooltip — what appears on hover
 Path — sequencing (line and polygon)
 Shape — only with shape mark type

 Each mark card slot creates a visual channel

PAGES card (less common):
 Adds animation control: Play, pause, speed, history trail

Show Me panel

Right side of workspace; toggle via Show Me button

Auto-suggests chart types based on selected fields
 - Available types highlighted
 - Unavailable types greyed out with explanation on hover
 - Click a type → Tableau rebuilds the viz

Required fields per chart (highlighted at bottom of Show Me):
 Bar: 1+ dimension, 1+ measure
 Line: 1 date, 1+ measure
 Scatter: 2 measures
 Map: 1 geo field, 1+ measure (optional)
 Text table: 1+ dimension, 1+ measure
 Heatmap: 2 dimensions, 1+ measure

Useful when:
 - You don't know which chart to use
 - You have selected fields but unsure how to combine them
 - You want to switch chart types quickly

The viz canvas

The main center area where your visualization appears

Key elements:
 - Axes (from Rows and Columns shelves)
 - Marks (bars, points, lines based on data)
 - Headers (category labels)
 - Legend (color/size encoding)
 - Title (worksheet name; customizable)

Interaction with the viz:
 - Hover: tooltip
 - Click: select a mark (filters via mark)
 - Right-click: context menu
 - Drag: pan the view
 - Scroll: zoom (when applicable)

The view can be:
 - Standard — auto-fits to data
 - Fit Width — full width
 - Fit Height — full height
 - Entire View — fits both dimensions
 - Normal — no auto-fit

Sheet tabs (bottom)

Each tab represents one of:
 - Worksheet (single visualization)
 - Dashboard (combination of sheets)
 - Story (sequence of dashboards/sheets)

Icons:
 Bar chart — worksheet
 Grid — dashboard
 Storyboard — story

Tab actions (right-click):
 Rename
 Duplicate
 Copy
 Hide / Show
 Delete
 Color (organization)

Far-left button: Data Source tab
 Returns to the data source setup screen

Far-right buttons:
 New Worksheet
 New Dashboard
 New Story

The Data Source page

Click "Data Source" tab at bottom-left

Three main areas:
 Top-left: Connections list (data sources you've connected to)
 Top-right: Data preview / canvas
 Bottom: Tables / sheets selected for use

Canvas:
 Drag tables / sheets here
 Set up joins or relationships between them
 Filter or rename tables

Preview (bottom):
 Shows sample of data after joins / filters
 Can rename columns, change data types, hide fields

Buttons:
 - Sheet 1 (return to first worksheet)
 - Extract / Live (connection mode)
 - Add filters at data source level

Connection mode: Live vs Extract

ModeBehaviorUse when
LiveQueries source on every actionReal-time data; small datasets; transactional DBs
ExtractSnapshot in Hyper file; refresh on schedulePerformance; offline work; large datasets

Switch between modes on Data Source page; for extracts, choose filters, aggregations, and incremental refresh policy.

Toolbar key buttons

Most commonly used (left to right):

 📁 Save / Save As
 📂 Open workbook
 ➕ New worksheet
 ↺ Undo
 ↻ Redo
 ✗ Clear sheet
 🔄 Refresh data source
 ⇄ Swap rows and columns (Ctrl+W)
 ↕ Sort ascending / descending
 ⬇ Format
 📦 Group
 💡 Highlight selected
 📏 Fit (Standard / Fit Width / Fit Height / Entire View)
 ⬛ Presentation mode (full screen)
 📤 Share / Publish

Keyboard shortcuts:
 Ctrl+S — Save
 Ctrl+Z — Undo
 Ctrl+W — Swap rows/columns
 F7 — Presentation mode
 Alt+Shift+drag — duplicate field
 Ctrl+drag — copy

Common interface mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Putting a measure on Columns/Rows expecting categorical layout — measures aggregate by default
  2. Forgetting the Marks card per-sheet — each sheet has independent Marks card configuration
  3. Confusing Filter shelf with Marks card Color — Filter restricts data; Color encodes
  4. Not knowing where to find a feature — most options are right-click menus
  5. Dragging field to Pages thinking it filters — Pages creates an animated slideshow
  6. Treating discrete blue field and continuous green field the same — different visual behavior
  7. Confusing the Worksheet, Dashboard, Story icons at bottom
  8. Forgetting to switch to Data Source tab when troubleshooting connections
  9. Closing the Data pane by accident — re-open via View menu
  10. Editing in a "Dashboard" sheet expecting filter behavior of a "Worksheet"
★ ON THE EXAM

"Where are fields listed?" → Data pane (left side).

"Drag fields here for x-axis?" → Columns shelf.

"Drag fields here for y-axis?" → Rows shelf.

"Filter the data shown?" → Filters shelf.

"Animate over a field?" → Pages shelf.

"Encode color/size/label?" → Marks card.

"Chart suggestions?" → Show Me panel.

"Switch chart type?" → Marks card → mark type dropdown.

"Each sheet has its own?" → Marks card (and shelves).

"Dimensions vs measures?" → Categorical (blue, above line) vs numeric (green, below).

"Discrete vs continuous?" → Blue pills (headers) vs green pills (axes).

"Swap rows and columns?" → Ctrl+W or toolbar swap button.

"Configure data source?" → Data Source tab at bottom.

"Live vs extract toggle?" → Top-right of Data Source page.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Data pane (left) lists fields: Dimensions (blue, categorical, above line) and Measures (green, numeric, below)
  • Field icons indicate type: Abc (string), # (number), 📅 (date), 🌍 (geo), T/F (boolean), = (calculated)
  • Shelves: Columns (x), Rows (y), Filters (subset data), Pages (animate)
  • Marks card controls visual encoding: Color, Size, Label, Detail, Tooltip, Shape, Path
  • Each sheet has its own independent Marks card configuration
  • Mark type dropdown: Bar, Line, Area, Circle, Shape, Text, Map, Pie, Gantt, Polygon, Density
  • Show Me panel suggests chart types based on currently selected fields
  • Bottom tabs: Worksheet (single viz), Dashboard (combine), Story (narrate sequence)
  • Data Source tab returns to the connection setup screen
  • Live mode queries source live; Extract mode uses a Hyper snapshot
  • Swap rows and columns: Ctrl+W or toolbar button
  • Presentation mode: F7 (full screen, hides editing)
  • Right-click is your friend — most options live in context menus
  • Same field can appear blue (discrete) or green (continuous) on shelves
  • Drag dimensions to break the viz into categories; drag measures to aggregate values

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tableau's two-by-two classification — dimension/measure × discrete/continuous — controls everything about how a field behaves in a viz. The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam tests this distinction directly, repeatedly.

The two classifications

FOUR FIELD STATES
Every field on a shelf has TWO independent properties:

1. Dimension vs Measure — what the field IS
  Dimension: categorical (used to slice)
  Measure: numeric (used to aggregate)

2. Discrete vs Continuous — how the field BEHAVES on the shelf
  Discrete (blue): finite distinct values → creates headers
  Continuous (green): unbroken range → creates an axis

Both properties can be switched independently.

Dimension vs Measure

DimensionMeasure
Qualitative / categorical / descriptiveQuantitative / numerical / aggregatable
Above the dividing line in Data paneBelow the dividing line
Drag to shelf → slices the viz (groups rows)Drag to shelf → aggregates (default SUM)
Examples: Region, Product, Customer Name, Order DateExamples: Sales, Profit, Quantity, Tax
Generally don't change when you slice/diceNumbers that get summed/averaged/counted

Converting between dimension and measure

Tableau auto-classifies but you can override:

Convert measure to dimension:
 When numeric IDs should be categorical (e.g., Customer ID, Product ID)
 Right-click field in Data pane → Convert to Dimension
 Or on a shelf: right-click pill → Convert to Dimension

Convert dimension to measure:
 Rare; usually applies when a calculated dimension should aggregate
 Right-click → Convert to Measure

Common need:
 Order ID, ZIP Code, Year, Customer ID
 These are NUMERIC but should be DIMENSIONS (we don't sum ZIP codes)
 Convert on first use; the change persists in the workbook

Discrete vs Continuous

Discrete (blue)Continuous (green)
Distinct, finite valuesUnbroken range of values
Creates HEADERS on vizCreates an AXIS on viz
Sorted alphabetically/numerically by valueSorted by position on axis
Each value is a categoryValues fall on a number line
Example: Region (4 values)Example: Sales ($0 - $1,000,000)

The four combinations

DIMENSION + DISCRETE (most common dim usage)
 Region pill: blue
 Creates row/column headers (East, West, North, South)
 Examples: Region, Product, Customer Name, Status

DIMENSION + CONTINUOUS (less common)
 Date can be continuous as a timeline
 Creates an unbroken axis (date scale)
 Examples: Year as continuous → date axis instead of header per year

MEASURE + CONTINUOUS (default measure usage)
 Sales pill: green
 Creates an axis (e.g., $0 to $100K)
 Examples: SUM(Sales), AVG(Discount)

MEASURE + DISCRETE (uncommon but useful)
 Like a "bin" — treats each value as its own header
 Useful for: showing individual unaggregated numeric values as labels
 Example: discrete YEAR(Order Date) breaks chart into yearly headers

Dates — the trickiest type

Dates can be DISCRETE or CONTINUOUS, with DATE PART or DATE VALUE

DATE PARTS (discrete usage):
 Year, Quarter, Month, Week, Day
 Each is a NAME / NUMBER (e.g., "January", 1, 2, 3...)
 Creates headers
 Same months across years combine (Jan 2023 + Jan 2024 → "January")

DATE VALUES (continuous usage):
 Year, Quarter, Month, Day (same options, but as continuous)
 Each is a DATE (e.g., 2023-01-01)
 Creates a continuous time axis
 Year 2023 and Year 2024 are different points on axis

When you drag a date:
 Default: discrete YEAR (blue)
 Right-click → Discrete vs Continuous toggle
 Right-click → choose date part vs date value

Visual difference:
 Discrete date: bar chart with gaps between years
 Continuous date: line chart with smooth time axis

Default aggregations

When a measure is placed on a shelf, Tableau auto-aggregates

Default: SUM(field)

Other aggregations (right-click pill → Measure):
 Sum, Average, Median
 Count, Count Distinct
 Min, Max
 Standard Deviation, Variance
 Percentile

Disaggregate:
 Analysis menu → uncheck "Aggregate Measures"
 Now every row appears as its own mark
 Use case: scatter plots, individual transactions

Default agg per field:
 Right-click field in Data pane → Default Properties → Aggregation
 Set the workbook-wide default (e.g., Sales always averaged)

Switching between discrete and continuous

On a shelf:
 Right-click the pill → toggle Discrete / Continuous
 OR drag while holding Shift (varies by version)

Visual feedback:
 Blue pill = discrete (header)
 Green pill = continuous (axis)

Examples:
 Year as discrete: 2022 | 2023 | 2024 (separate columns)
 Year as continuous: line plot from 2022 to 2024

 SUM(Sales) as continuous (default): green axis
 SUM(Sales) as discrete: each value becomes a label (rare)

Common pattern for time series:
 Continuous MONTH(Order Date) on Columns
 Continuous SUM(Sales) on Rows
 Mark type: Line

Visual axis vs headers

DISCRETE creates HEADERS:
 Each value gets its own slot
 Categorical layout (bar chart, table)
 Order: alphabetical or by sort
 Spacing: equal between values

 Region | East | West | North | South
 Sales | 100 | 80 | 60 | 50

CONTINUOUS creates an AXIS:
 Numeric scale; values placed proportionally
 Continuous layout (line, scatter)
 Order: numeric
 Spacing: proportional to value

 Sales axis: $0 $50 $100 $150 $200
 ────────────●────●─────────●────────●

A pill can be on Rows or Columns; behavior follows discrete/continuous

Why this matters — visualization choice

Bar chart with year:
 Discrete YEAR → gaps between years; classic bar chart
 Continuous YEAR → bars on a date axis (less common)

Line chart with year:
 Continuous YEAR(date) preferred — smooth time axis
 Discrete YEAR works but feels stepped

Scatter plot:
 Both axes need to be CONTINUOUS measures
 Disaggregate measures via Analysis → Aggregate Measures off
 Each row becomes a dot at its (x, y) position

Map:
 Need geographic role assignment
 Both Latitude and Longitude continuous

Crosstab / text table:
 Discrete dimensions on Rows and Columns
 Aggregated measure on Text (Marks card)

Worked example — same field, different views

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Order Date in three forms
// Same field: Order Date
// Three different viz outcomes:

// 1. YEAR as DISCRETE on Columns + SUM(Sales) on Rows
// Result: Three separate bars labeled 2022, 2023, 2024
// Each bar's height = total sales for that year
// Gaps between bars (categorical)

// 2. YEAR as CONTINUOUS on Columns + SUM(Sales) on Rows
// Result: Line chart from 2022 to 2024 (no gaps)
// X-axis is a continuous date scale
// More natural for trends

// 3. MONTH (Date Part, DISCRETE) on Columns + SUM(Sales) on Rows
// Result: 12 bars labeled Jan-Dec
// SUMS across all years (Jan 2022 + Jan 2023 + Jan 2024 combined)
// Shows seasonality

// 4. MONTH (Date Value, CONTINUOUS) on Columns + SUM(Sales) on Rows
// Result: Continuous time axis from earliest to latest date
// Shows month-by-month sequence (Jan-22, Feb-22, ... Dec-24)
// Best for trend visualization with monthly granularity

// 5. WEEKDAY (Date Part, DISCRETE) — Mon, Tue, ..., Sun
// SUMS across all weeks
// Shows day-of-week patterns

// Switching:
// Right-click the pill → choose Year / Quarter / Month / Week / Day
// → choose Date Part vs Date Value (discrete vs continuous)

Common dimension/measure mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Treating Customer ID as a measure — convert to dimension
  2. Year aggregated as SUM — Sum(2024) = 2024; meaningless. Convert to dimension
  3. Continuous date on a bar chart — usually wanted discrete
  4. Discrete date on a line chart — usually wanted continuous
  5. Forgetting that SUM is the default agg — Tableau auto-sums numeric measures
  6. Wanting median but plotting SUM by accident — right-click pill → Measure → Median
  7. Confusing date part vs date value — part = name; value = actual date
  8. Want unaggregated data? Analysis menu → uncheck Aggregate Measures
  9. Wrong field type in calculation — IF [Score] = "A" but Score is numeric → no rows
  10. Postal/ZIP codes as measures — make them dimensions
★ ON THE EXAM

"Dimension?" → Categorical, qualitative, descriptive.

"Measure?" → Numerical, quantitative, aggregatable.

"Blue pill?" → Discrete (creates headers).

"Green pill?" → Continuous (creates axis).

"Default aggregation?" → SUM.

"Change aggregation?" → Right-click pill → Measure → choose.

"Convert measure to dimension?" → Right-click field → Convert to Dimension.

"Year on bar chart?" → Usually discrete dimension.

"Year on line chart?" → Usually continuous date value.

"Date part?" → Just the part name (e.g., "January" or "1" for month).

"Date value?" → Full date corresponding to that part (e.g., 2024-01-01 for Jan 2024).

"Disaggregate?" → Analysis → uncheck Aggregate Measures.

"Default for new field?" → Right-click → Default Properties → Aggregation.

"Sum of January across years?" → Date Part MONTH (discrete).

"Each Jan-2024 / Feb-2024 separate?" → Date Value MONTH (continuous).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Every field has TWO properties: dimension/measure (what it is) and discrete/continuous (how it behaves)
  • Dimensions: categorical, qualitative (Region, Product); used to slice
  • Measures: numeric, quantitative (Sales, Profit); used to aggregate
  • Discrete pills are blue → create headers; sorted alphabetically/numerically
  • Continuous pills are green → create axes; positioned numerically on scale
  • The dividing line in the Data pane separates Dimensions (above) from Measures (below)
  • Convert types: right-click field → Convert to Dimension / Measure
  • Switch discrete/continuous: right-click pill on shelf → toggle
  • Default measure aggregation is SUM; change via right-click pill → Measure
  • Date Parts are discrete name/number values (e.g., "January", 1); Date Values are continuous dates (e.g., 2024-01-01)
  • Date Part MONTH discrete: sums across years for each month name
  • Date Value MONTH continuous: each month-year as a separate point
  • Convert numeric IDs (Customer ID, ZIP) to dimensions to prevent SUM-by-default
  • Disaggregate via Analysis → uncheck Aggregate Measures (shows individual rows)
  • Same field can appear in multiple states on different shelves — pills are independent

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tableau supports 100+ data connectors. Choosing the right one and the right connection mode determines what's possible downstream. The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam tests common connectors and live vs extract.

Starting a new connection

When Tableau Desktop opens:
 Start Page shows recent files + Connect panel

Connect panel (left side):
 To a File
 - Microsoft Excel
 - Text file (CSV, TSV, TXT)
 - Microsoft Access

Combining tables is one of Tableau's core operations. In 2020.2, Tableau introduced Relationships (the new default) alongside Joins. They behave differently, and knowing when to use each is exam material.

Three ways to combine tables

MethodWhenSQL equivalent
RelationshipLogical, on-demand joins (2020.2+; default)Context-dependent JOIN
JoinCombine into single physical tableJOIN (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL)
UnionStack tables vertically (same schema)UNION ALL

Relationships — the modern default

Introduced in Tableau 2020.2; now the default when you drag tables to canvas

How they work:
 - Tables stay LOGICALLY separate (no physical join)
 - Tableau decides the right join at QUERY TIME based on what's in the viz
 - Each viz can use a different join automatically
 - Like Power BI relationships

Set up:
 Drag second table to canvas → noodle (line) appears connecting them
 Click noodle → configure:
 - Performance Options (cardinality, referential integrity)
 - Join keys (multiple supported)

Benefits over Joins:
 - No duplication when fact tables have different granularity
 - No "fan-out" inflation of aggregations
 - Different metrics from different tables can be displayed together cleanly
 - Tableau picks the right join per viz (inner / left / outer)

Cardinality settings (Performance Options):
 - Many or One (typical: many on fact, one on dim)
 - Referential integrity: All records match? (enables INNER join optimization)

Joins — physical combination

Pre-2020.2 default; still available

How to use Joins instead of Relationships:
 Drag tables to canvas → connect with relationship
 DOUBLE-CLICK a table to enter the PHYSICAL layer
 Drag the second table INTO the open box (not as a separate node)
 Now you're creating a true JOIN

Join types (icons on connector):
 Inner — rows matching in both
 Left — all rows from left + matching from right
 Right — all rows from right + matching from left
 Full outer — all rows from both (matched or not)

Join clauses:
 Click join icon → set conditions
 Multiple clauses (AND)
 Operators: =, <>, <, >, <=, >=

After join, both tables are merged into ONE logical table
All columns from both tables visible in Data pane

Relationships vs Joins — when to use which

★ MODERN GUIDANCE

Default to RELATIONSHIPS for most use cases.

Use JOINS when:

  • You need a specific join type forced for ALL queries
  • Combining tables from non-relational sources (some file types)
  • Building a single dimension table from multiple sources
  • Performance optimization with referential integrity guarantees

Use RELATIONSHIPS when:

  • You have multiple fact tables at different granularity
  • You want Tableau to optimize joins per viz
  • You need to avoid duplication/fan-out
  • You want a flexible, performant model

The fan-out problem (Joins) — why Relationships help

Classic problem with Joins:
 Orders (one per order)
 Order Items (many per order)
 
 JOIN them → each Order row duplicates per item
 SUM(Order_Total) → counts each order MULTIPLE times
 Result: inflated totals

Workaround with Joins:
 Use COUNTD or apply LOD expressions to deduplicate
 Complex; error-prone

With Relationships:
 Tableau queries each table at correct granularity
 SUM(Order_Total) → uses Orders table; gives correct total
 COUNT(Item_ID) → uses Items table; counts items
 Automatically chooses correct join per query

Key concept: Relationships handle multi-fact analysis natively.

Union — stacking tables

Union combines tables VERTICALLY (UNION ALL in SQL)

Use cases:
 - Monthly CSV files (Jan, Feb, Mar...) → one combined table
 - Same schema across regions (NA, EMEA, APAC) → one combined view

Two ways:
 Manual:
 Drag table 1 to canvas
 Right-click → Convert to Union
 Drag additional tables into Union dialog
 Tableau matches columns BY NAME

 Wildcard:
 Same as above, but specify a pattern
 e.g., "Sales_*.csv" picks all CSVs matching pattern
 NEW files added later auto-included on next refresh

Field matching:
 - Same column names → combine into one column
 - Different column names → separate columns (nulls for missing)
 - Use Find Matching Fields button to align names

Source columns automatically added:
 Sheet — name of source sheet/table
 Path — file path (for file unions)
 Useful for tracing provenance

Wildcard union — auto-discovery

When connecting to Excel or file folder:
 Convert table to Union → choose Wildcard tab

Settings:
 Workbooks: which Excel files to scan
 Sheets: name pattern (e.g., "Sales_*")
 Search subfolders: yes/no
 
Match by:
 Workbook (file name)
 Sheet (sheet name)

Perfect for:
 Monthly drop folders (monthly file added; auto-included)
 Regional Excel workbooks following naming convention

Caveats:
 All matched files must have similar columns
 Bad outliers cause errors or odd nulls
 Test with sample first

Cross-database joins

Tableau supports joining tables from DIFFERENT data sources

Setup:
 Data Source page → add a second connection (top-left, click "Add" near Connections)
 Drag a table from the second connection onto the canvas
 Connect to existing table → join clause

How it works:
 Tableau brings the data into memory and joins locally
 Both sources must be accessible
 Performance: limited by slower source

Common scenario:
 Sales from SQL Server + Targets from Excel
 Join on Region key
 Compare actual vs target on dashboards

Distinction:
 Cross-database join = JOIN across sources (single logical table)
 Data blending = separate sources, joined per viz (covered next section)

Configuring relationships

Click the "noodle" between two tables in Relationship view

Edit Relationship dialog:
 Match fields: choose columns for the join
 Add multiple matches if composite key
 Operator: = (most common)

 Performance Options:
 Cardinality:
 Many - The relationship side has duplicates
 One - The relationship side is unique
 
 Referential Integrity:
 All records match - INNER join optimization enabled
 Some records don't match - LEFT/RIGHT join used

 Cardinality drives query optimization:
 Many-to-many is the safest default if unsure
 One-to-many (or many-to-one) lets Tableau do simpler queries

Best practice:
 Set cardinality and RI based on your knowledge of the data
 Wrong values can cause incorrect aggregations

Worked example — multi-table model

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sales analytics model
// Tables:
// Orders (one row per order)
// Order Items (one row per item)
// Products (one row per product)
// Customers (one row per customer)
// Date (one row per date)
// Targets (one row per region per month)

// With Relationships (modern, recommended):

// Connect Orders to Customers (cardinality: many → one)
// Orders.CustomerID = Customers.CustomerID

// Connect Orders to Order Items (one → many)
// Orders.OrderID = OrderItems.OrderID

// Connect Order Items to Products (many → one)
// OrderItems.ProductID = Products.ProductID

// Connect Orders to Date (many → one)
// Orders.OrderDate = Date.Date

// Now build vizzes freely:
// "SUM(Sales) by Customer Name"
// Uses Orders + Customers; correct totals
// "COUNT(Items) by Product"
// Uses OrderItems + Products
// "SUM(Sales) by Region by Quarter vs Target"
// Mix Orders + Date + Targets
// No fan-out, no manual LODs needed

// With Joins (old way; more brittle):
// Joining Orders + OrderItems duplicates Order totals
// Need DISTINCT or LOD expressions to deduplicate
// Multiple separate joins for different metrics
// Generally avoided post-2020.2 except for specific cases

Common join/relationship mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Joining fact tables at different granularity — use Relationships instead
  2. Using INNER join when LEFT would be correct — drops records silently
  3. Union with mismatched column names — gets extra columns with nulls
  4. Cross-database join when blending would be faster — see next section
  5. Wrong cardinality in Relationship — incorrect aggregations
  6. Assuming all records match without RI — incorrect inner join optimization
  7. Hardcoded wildcard pattern — fails when filename convention changes
  8. Joining to a giant table just to filter — pre-filter with custom SQL first
  9. Forgetting Sheet/Path columns in unions — useful for tracing source
  10. Editing relationship without testing — change cascades into all vizzes
★ ON THE EXAM

"Default since 2020.2?" → Relationships.

"Logical layer?" → Relationships (tables stay separate).

"Physical layer?" → Joins (combined into one table; double-click table to enter).

"4 join types?" → Inner, Left, Right, Full outer.

"Stack tables vertically?" → Union.

"Auto-include new monthly files?" → Wildcard union.

"Combine tables from different sources?" → Cross-database join or blending.

"Cross-database join location?" → Tableau handles in memory.

"Fan-out problem fix?" → Use Relationships (handles multi-granularity natively).

"Cardinality?" → Many or One per side; configurable in relationship options.

"Referential Integrity setting?" → "All records match" enables INNER join optimization.

"Multiple join keys?" → Composite key; add additional clauses in join setup.

"Provenance columns after Union?" → Sheet (table name), Path (file path).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Three ways to combine tables: Relationships, Joins, Union
  • Relationships (default since 2020.2): logical layer; tables stay separate; Tableau chooses join per query
  • Joins: physical layer; tables merged into one; specify type (Inner/Left/Right/Full)
  • To use Joins: double-click a table on canvas to enter physical layer
  • Union: vertical stacking of same-schema tables (UNION ALL in SQL)
  • Wildcard Union auto-includes new files matching a pattern
  • Sheet and Path columns auto-added during Union — useful for source tracing
  • Cross-database joins combine tables from different sources (in-memory)
  • Relationships avoid fan-out — query each table at correct granularity
  • Cardinality (Many/One) and Referential Integrity drive query optimization
  • Default to Relationships unless you specifically need physical Join behavior
  • Wrong cardinality settings cause incorrect aggregations
  • Multiple join keys: add additional match clauses in the join/relationship dialog
  • Joins must specify type and clauses explicitly
  • Pre-filter big tables via Data Source filters or custom SQL before joining

When combining data from multiple sources, you have three options: cross-database joins, relationships, or data blending. Each has different semantics and use cases. The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam tests blending mechanics specifically.

The three combination approaches

ApproachWhereUse case
Cross-database joinData Source page; one logical modelTables from different DBs treated as one
RelationshipData Source page; logical layerModern default; multi-granularity friendly
Data blendingPer-worksheet, two separate data sourcesQuick combine without merging models

Data blending fundamentals

Data blending: combine data from MULTIPLE data sources in a SINGLE viz

How it works:
 Primary data source (linked first in worksheet)
 Secondary data source (joined on common fields PER WORKSHEET)
 Blended LEFT join behavior — primary always wins; secondary fills in

Each worksheet has its own blend
 Sheet A might use Source1 as primary
 Sheet B might use Source2 as primary
 Tableau remembers per sheet

Where to set up:
 Sheet → Data pane → switch to secondary data source
 Look for orange ⛓ link icons next to common field names
 Click the link icon to activate the blend
 Now you can drag fields from BOTH sources into the viz

Primary vs secondary

Primary data source:
 First source dragged into the viz (or first selected)
 All dimensions in the viz come from this
 Determines the rows visible (LEFT side of the blend)
 Has a BLUE checkmark in the Data pane

Secondary data source:
 Second source; provides additional measures (and sometimes dimensions)
 Has an ORANGE checkmark when active in blend
 Aggregated TO the primary's granularity before display
 Cannot contribute dimensions to drill down beyond primary

To swap which is primary:
 Click the primary checkmark to deactivate
 Click another source's checkmark to make it primary
 All formulas referring to old primary need updating

Linking fields

Tableau auto-detects fields with the SAME NAME and TYPE as link candidates
 Date in primary + Date in secondary → auto-linkable

Visual indicator:
 Orange chain icon ⛓ next to field names in secondary
 Click to activate / deactivate

Manual linking:
 Data → Edit Blend Relationships
 Specify which fields in secondary map to which in primary
 Useful when names differ (e.g., "Region" vs "Sales Region")

Multiple link fields:
 All active links must match for a row to blend
 Like a composite key

Common linking pattern:
 Sales (primary) → Date, Region
 Targets (secondary) → Date, Region
 Blend on both → correct comparison

When to use blending vs cross-database join

Use blendingUse cross-database join
One source is at higher granularity (e.g., daily vs monthly targets)Both at same granularity
Different sheets need different combinationsNeed one unified model
Sources are very different in size (large primary, small secondary)Tables similar size
Need only some fields from secondaryNeed full access to secondary fields
Don't want to refresh both togetherWant them refreshed together

Blending limitations

⚠ KEY CONSTRAINTS

Blending has specific limits:

  • Secondary aggregates only: data from secondary always aggregated TO primary's granularity
  • Can't drill below primary's grain: secondary can't add detail that primary doesn't have
  • LEFT join semantics only: primary always retains all its rows
  • No row-level calculations across sources: only after aggregation
  • One-to-many from secondary: can cause unexpected duplication
  • Performance: data fetched from both sources per query
  • Per-sheet: blends don't share across sheets automatically

Worked example — sales vs targets

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Blend daily sales with monthly targets
// Setup:
// Primary data source: Sales (daily, by Region and Product)
// Date, Region, Product, Sales
// Secondary data source: Targets (monthly, by Region)
// Year, Month, Region, Target

// Common link fields: Region (and time roll-up)

// Step 1: Add both data sources to workbook
// Connect → To a File → Sales.xlsx
// Add another connection → Targets.xlsx (separate Connection group)

// Step 2: In worksheet, use Sales as primary
// Drag Sales[Region] to Rows
// Drag Sales[Sales] to Text

// Step 3: Switch to Targets data source (top of Data pane)
// Click the orange chain icon next to Region → activates blend
// Drag Targets[Target] to Text

// Result: matrix with Region | SUM(Sales) | SUM(Target)
// Sales rolled up by Region (Sales is primary)
// Target aggregated to match (one target value per region per query)

// Step 4: Date dimension blending
// Daily Sales linked to Targets[Month] requires careful linking
// Use Tableau's auto-detection on Year, Month
// Or create matching calculated fields in both sources

// Caveat: if Targets table has multiple rows per region (one per month)
// And primary aggregates to a single row per region
// Then Tableau aggregates the multiple targets (sum or avg)
// May want to filter Targets by date first to match
//
// Alternative: Build with relationship if both tables in same source
// Cleaner, no manual blend setup needed

Editing blend relationships

Data menu → Edit Blend Relationships

Dialog shows:
 Primary data source
 Each secondary source with editable mappings

For each secondary source:
 Default link fields (auto-detected matches)
 Custom link fields (manually specified)
 Add / Remove links

Why customize:
 Field names differ (e.g., "Region" vs "Sales Region")
 Want to disable an auto-link
 Composite keys needed (link on Region AND Date)

Check which links are active in viz:
 Data pane shows orange chain icons on linked fields
 Click to activate/deactivate per worksheet

Blending with calculated fields

In blended worksheets, you can reference fields from secondary
 Prefix with data source name and dot syntax
 Or use ATTR() for non-aggregable secondary dimensions

Example:
 // In primary data source, calculate variance
 Sales vs Target =
 SUM([Sales]) - SUM([Targets].[Target])

 Note: [Targets].[Target] references the secondary source

 // Variance percentage
 Variance Pct =
 DIVIDE(SUM([Sales]) - SUM([Targets].[Target]),
 SUM([Targets].[Target]))

ATTR() for dimensions in secondary:
 Use when secondary dimension may have multiple values per row
 Returns the value if unique, else *
 
 // Show country if uniquely determined; else *
 ATTR([Targets].[Country])

Common blending mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Treating secondary as primary — first-dragged source is primary
  2. Trying to drill below primary's grain — blending can't add detail beyond primary
  3. Forgetting orange chain icon — link not active means no blend
  4. Auto-detect wrong link — manually edit blend relationships
  5. Multiple secondary rows per primary key — secondary aggregates unexpectedly
  6. Blending when relationships would work — relationships often cleaner if in same source
  7. Performance issues with large secondary — Tableau queries secondary per viz
  8. Calculated field in secondary used as dimension — needs ATTR() in many cases
  9. Date hierarchies not matching grains — match daily-to-daily or roll up explicitly
  10. Per-sheet differences not realized — each sheet has independent blend
★ ON THE EXAM

"Where is data blending set up?" → Per worksheet.

"How are blending links visualized?" → Orange chain icon next to field.

"Primary determined by?" → First data source used in the viz.

"Secondary fields in calculations?" → Use [Source].[Field] dot notation.

"Aggregate dimension from secondary?" → ATTR().

"Join type semantics of blend?" → LEFT join only.

"Edit which fields link?" → Data → Edit Blend Relationships.

"Can secondary drill below primary?" → No; secondary aggregates to primary's grain.

"Difference vs cross-database join?" → Blend is per-sheet, aggregates secondary; cross-database is unified model.

"Performance concern?" → Each sheet queries both sources.

"Multiple linking fields?" → Composite key; all must match.

"Swap primary?" → Deactivate current; activate another source.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Data blending combines two data sources per worksheet (not in the data model)
  • First source used is primary (blue check); subsequent are secondary (orange check)
  • Orange chain icons indicate fields available for blending (auto-detected by name and type)
  • Blend semantics: LEFT join only — primary keeps all rows; secondary fills in
  • Secondary data is always aggregated to primary's granularity
  • Cannot drill below primary's level of detail using secondary alone
  • Reference secondary fields in calcs: [Source].[Field]
  • Use ATTR() for secondary dimensions to handle multi-value cases
  • Per-worksheet: each sheet has its own blend; can use different primaries
  • Edit Blend Relationships (Data menu) to customize field mappings
  • Use blending when: different granularity, occasional combination, different sources
  • Use cross-database join when: unified model needed, both same granularity
  • Use relationships when: tables in same model and you want flexibility
  • Common case: daily sales (primary) + monthly targets (secondary)
  • Verify blend is active by orange chain icon on key fields

Tableau's analytical power assumes data is in TIDY (long) format. Real data often arrives wide, messy, or mixed. The Pivot, Split, and Data Interpreter features let you clean up at connect time, before building any vizzes.

Pivoting wide to long

PIVOT IN TABLEAU
Tableau prefers LONG format: one column per variable, one row per observation.

Wide format: Year | Jan | Feb | Mar
Long format: Year | Month | Sales

Pivot converts wide → long. Tableau's Pivot feature combines selected columns into key-value pairs. 
Setup:
 Data Source page → preview pane (bottom)
 Select multiple columns (Ctrl+click headers)
 Right-click → Pivot

Result:
 Selected columns become rows
 Two new columns: "Pivot Field Names" and "Pivot Field Values"
 Rename these to meaningful names ("Month" and "Sales" in example)

Example:
 Year | Jan_Sales | Feb_Sales | Mar_Sales
 2024 | 100 | 200 | 150

 After pivot of Jan_Sales, Feb_Sales, Mar_Sales:
 Year | Pivot Field Names | Pivot Field Values
 2024 | Jan_Sales | 100
 2024 | Feb_Sales | 200
 2024 | Mar_Sales | 150

 Rename → Month and Sales
 Now you can build viz with Month on Columns, SUM(Sales) on Rows

Reverse pivot — long to wide

Tableau doesn't have a native "unpivot to wide" in Data Source page
 (unlike Power Query's Pivot Column)

Workarounds:
 - Tableau Prep Builder has explicit pivot rows-to-columns
 - Build the wide structure in the viz itself (Columns + measure)
 - Use FIXED LOD expressions to create per-category measures

For exam purposes:
 Just know Tableau's Pivot defaults wide → long
 And the result columns are "Pivot Field Names" and "Pivot Field Values"

Splitting columns

Split a column into multiple based on delimiter or position

Methods:
 Right-click column in preview → Split
 Auto-detects delimiter (most common one)
 Creates as many new columns as needed
 Result: "Column - Split 1", "Column - Split 2", ...

 Right-click column → Custom Split
 Specify delimiter and split count
 Example: split "FirstName-LastName-MiddleInitial" on "-" into 3 columns

Calculated field SPLIT function:
 // Get part #N from a delimited string
 [Full Name] split " " 1 → FirstName
 [Full Name] split " " 2 → LastName

 Or function syntax:
 SPLIT([Full Name], " ", 1)
 SPLIT([Full Name], " ", -1) // last token

Use cases:
 - Email → username + domain
 - Address → street + city + zip
 - Full Name → first + last
 - Filename → category + timestamp

The Data Interpreter

For messy Excel files (headers in middle, sub-tables, formatting cruft)

Activate:
 Top of Data Source page → check "Use Data Interpreter"

What it cleans up:
 - Removes title rows above headers
 - Removes summary/totals rows below data
 - Detects and removes sub-tables embedded in one sheet
 - Strips blank rows / columns
 - Identifies the "real" header row

After interpretation:
 Side panel shows "Review the results"
 Click to see what Data Interpreter changed
 Accept (default) or untoggle to revert

When to use:
 Almost always on Excel files
 Especially: financial reports with titles, line items, totals
 Reports formatted for humans, not data tools

Not for:
 Already-clean tabular data
 CSV files (rare to need)

Data type conversion

In Data Source preview, each column has a type icon at the top

Click icon → choose:
 Number (decimal)
 Number (whole)
 Date & Time
 Date
 String
 Boolean
 Geographic role (City, State, Country, etc.)

Why change:
 Postal codes as Number → leading zeros lost
 Year as Number → averages weirdly
 Dates as String → no date features (DATEPART won't work)
 Geographic fields → enables map visualization

Geographic roles:
 City, Country / Region, State / Province, ZIP Code / Postcode, Area Code,
 Congressional District (US), County, NUTS Europe, CBSA / MSA
 Latitude (auto-generated if geo recognized), Longitude (same)

Renaming and hiding columns

Renaming in Data Source preview:
 Double-click column header → type new name
 Or: right-click → Rename

Renaming in Data pane (after entering worksheet):
 Right-click field → Rename

Hiding columns:
 Right-click in Data Source → Hide
 Hidden columns excluded from extract
 Smaller files, faster queries

When to hide:
 - Internal IDs / foreign keys (still usable for joining)
 - Audit fields (created_by, updated_at) not needed for analysis
 - Redundant fields (you have both raw and calculated)

Unhide:
 Data Source page → top right → "Show hidden columns"

Aliases — display names for values

Change how individual values DISPLAY without changing the data

Right-click a dimension field → Aliases
 See: list of values + alias columns
 Edit aliases per value:
 Raw value: "F" → Alias: "Female"
 Raw value: "M" → Alias: "Male"

Use cases:
 - Codes to friendly names (M → Male, F → Female, 1 → Active, 0 → Inactive)
 - Translation between systems
 - Better tooltips and labels

Aliases don't affect calculations (calcs still use raw values)
Workbook-specific; doesn't change underlying data

Cleanup operations summary

OperationLocation
Auto-clean messy ExcelUse Data Interpreter checkbox
Wide → longRight-click selected columns → Pivot
Split one column into manyRight-click column → Split / Custom Split
Change data typeClick type icon at top of column
Assign geographic roleSame icon → Geographic role
Rename columnDouble-click header
Hide columnRight-click → Hide
Alias a valueRight-click field → Aliases
Group multiple valuesRight-click field → Group (covered later)

Tableau Prep Builder — for serious cleaning

When data needs MORE cleaning than Data Source page provides:
 Use Tableau Prep Builder (separate paid tool, included with Creator license)

Prep Builder capabilities:
 - Visual flow-based pipeline
 - Cleaning steps: clean, group, split, replace, pivot, aggregate, join, union
 - Output: published data source or .hyper file
 - Schedule via Prep Conductor (Server add-on)

Use Prep instead of Power Query / SQL when:
 - You want visual ETL
 - Logic is too complex for Data Source page
 - Many sources need combined cleaning
 - You'll reuse the cleaned data across workbooks

For exam: just know Tableau Prep exists and complements Desktop
 Tableau Desktop = analysis; Tableau Prep = data preparation

Worked example — clean and pivot retail data

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Messy retail Excel
// Raw file: Monthly_Sales_2024.xlsx
//
// Sheet content:
// Row 1: "Q1 2024 Sales Report"
// Row 2: blank
// Row 3: "Source: ERP Export"
// Row 4: blank
// Row 5: Region | Store | Jan | Feb | Mar | Total
// Rows 6-50: data
// Row 51: blank
// Row 52: "Total" with column sums

// Steps:

// 1. Connect to Excel file
// 2. Enable Data Interpreter
// → Strips rows 1-4 (titles) and row 51-52 (totals)
// → Detects header at row 5

// 3. Pivot the month columns
// Select Jan, Feb, Mar columns
// Right-click → Pivot
// Result: Pivot Field Names (= "Jan", "Feb", etc.)
// Pivot Field Values (= the numbers)

// 4. Rename pivot columns
// "Pivot Field Names" → "Month"
// "Pivot Field Values" → "Sales"

// 5. Hide the Total column (not needed; will recompute in Tableau)

// 6. Set Region's geographic role
// Click type icon → Geographic role → State / Province

// 7. Add a Year column with a calculated field
// Calculated field "Year" = 2024 (constant for this file)

// 8. Optional: Union with monthly_sales_2023.xlsx for multi-year analysis

// Now ready to build vizzes:
// - SUM(Sales) by Month by Region (line chart)
// - Filled map of Region with Sales

Common cleanup mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Skipping Data Interpreter on Excel files — try it before manual cleaning
  2. Not pivoting wide data — leaves you stuck with each month as a measure
  3. Forgetting to rename "Pivot Field Names" / "Pivot Field Values"
  4. Postal codes left as Number type — loses leading zeros
  5. Date stored as String — no date functions work; convert first
  6. Forgetting to assign geographic role — maps don't recognize fields
  7. Hiding columns then needing them later — Show hidden columns toggle
  8. Aliases instead of calculated fields — for simple display only; calcs still use raw
  9. Reading messy data into Desktop instead of Prep — Prep is better for complex flows
  10. Split when SPLIT function would work in calc — calc is dynamic; Split is one-time
★ ON THE EXAM

"Wide → long?" → Pivot (right-click selected columns).

"Pivot result columns?" → "Pivot Field Names" + "Pivot Field Values".

"Auto-clean Excel?" → Data Interpreter (checkbox at top).

"Split column?" → Right-click → Split (auto-detect) or Custom Split.

"Calc to split?" → SPLIT(string, delimiter, position).

"Change data type?" → Click type icon at column header.

"Enable maps?" → Assign Geographic role to location field.

"Display alternate value text?" → Aliases (per value).

"Hide column from extract?" → Right-click → Hide.

"Postal code best type?" → String (preserves leading zeros).

"Date functions need?" → Date or DateTime type.

"Beyond Data Source cleaning?" → Tableau Prep Builder.

"Reverse pivot (long → wide)?" → Tableau Prep or build in viz; no direct Desktop option.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Tableau prefers long (tidy) format: one column per variable, one row per observation
  • Pivot converts wide → long: select multiple columns, right-click, Pivot
  • Pivot result has two new columns: "Pivot Field Names" and "Pivot Field Values" — rename them
  • No direct long → wide in Desktop; use Tableau Prep or build in viz
  • Split column: auto-detect delimiter, or use Custom Split for precise control
  • SPLIT() function in calculated fields for dynamic split
  • Data Interpreter auto-cleans messy Excel: titles, totals, sub-tables, blank rows
  • Change data type via the icon at top of each column (Number, Date, String, Boolean)
  • Geographic roles: City, State, Country, ZIP, etc. — enables map visualization
  • Rename columns by double-clicking header
  • Hide columns to keep them out of extracts; restore via "Show hidden columns"
  • Aliases change display values without affecting underlying data
  • For complex cleaning across many sources, use Tableau Prep Builder
  • Postal codes should be String to preserve leading zeros
  • Dates as Strings prevent date functions — convert type first

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tableau's strength is building visualizations fast. The Show Me panel suggests appropriate charts based on your fields, and understanding the common chart types — and how Tableau constructs them — is essential. The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam asks "what chart fits this data?" frequently.

The Show Me panel

Right side of workspace; toggle via Show Me button

Auto-suggests chart types based on:
 Currently selected fields in Data pane
 Currently placed pills on shelves

Each chart icon has hover text showing:
 Required fields (e.g., "1 dimension, 1 measure")
 Optional fields (additional aggregations)

Highlighted icons:
 Available with current fields
 Click to apply

Greyed-out icons:
 Require different fields
 Hover for explanation

The "Show Me" recommended chart for your selection appears highlighted with a border

Bar chart — the workhorse

Required: 0+ dimension, 1+ measure (or vice versa)

How to build:
 Drag dimension to Columns or Rows
 Drag measure to Rows or Columns (the other shelf)
 Mark type: Bar

Variations:
 Vertical bar (column chart): dimension on Columns, measure on Rows
 Horizontal bar: dimension on Rows, measure on Columns (recommended for many categories)
 Stacked bar: add a second dimension to Color on Marks card
 Side-by-side bar: add second dimension to Columns or Rows
 100% stacked: right-click measure → Quick Table Calc → Percent of Total

Sort the bars:
 Click sort icons in toolbar (alphabetical or by measure)
 Right-click dimension pill → Sort → Field → SUM(Sales) → Descending

When to use:
 Comparing values across categories — the most universal chart

Line chart — trends over time

Required: 1 date dimension (continuous), 1+ measure

How to build:
 Drag Date to Columns; right-click → Continuous + Date Value
 Drag Measure to Rows
 Mark type: Line (or auto-detects)

Multiple lines (series):
 Add a dimension to Color on Marks card
 Each value in dimension becomes a line

Variations:
 Stepped line: Marks card → Path → Step
 Jump line: Marks card → Path → Jump
 Smoothed: Analysis → Trend Lines

When to use:
 Trends over continuous time
 Comparing trajectories across multiple categories

Pie chart and Donut

Required: 1 dimension, 1 measure

How to build:
 Mark type: Pie
 Drag dimension to Color (Marks card)
 Drag measure to Angle (Marks card)
 Adjust Size to make slices bigger
 Add measure to Label for value display

Donut chart (no built-in):
 Two synchronized pies layered with one hidden in center
 Use dual axis trick:
 Drag MIN(1) to Rows twice
 Make both axes Pies
 Second pie: white circle covering center
 Dual axis: right-click second axis → Dual Axis
 Synchronize axis (right-click)
 Result: donut

Caveat:
 Pie charts work for ≤ 5 slices
 More → use bar or treemap instead

Scatter plot — relationships

Required: 2 measures (one on each axis)

How to build:
 Drag Measure 1 to Columns
 Drag Measure 2 to Rows
 Mark type: Circle (or Shape)
 Default: single mark (aggregated total)
 
Disaggregate to see individual rows:
 Analysis → uncheck "Aggregate Measures"
 Each row becomes a point

Add encodings:
 Color: dimension → categorical groups
 Size: additional measure → bubble size
 Label: identify points
 Shape: change marker style

Variations:
 Bubble chart: scatter + Size encoding (3rd measure)
 Trend line: Analysis → Trend Lines → Show Trend Lines

When to use:
 Correlation between two metrics
 Outlier detection
 Customer segmentation (e.g., spend vs frequency)

Maps — spatial analysis

Required: 1 geographic field

How to build:
 Drag geographic field to canvas (Country / State / City)
 Tableau auto-recognizes if Data Type → Geographic Role is set
 Latitude (generated), Longitude (generated) auto-added

Map types (Marks card):
 Map — filled regions (choropleth)
 Symbol Map — bubbles at points
 Density — heat map by point density

For filled map:
 Drag measure to Color
 Each region colored by value

For bubble map:
 Mark type: Circle
 Drag measure to Size
 Optionally, second measure to Color

Custom geocoding:
 Map menu → Geocoding → Import custom geocoding
 For non-standard regions (ZIP+4, custom territories)

Map options:
 Map → Map Layers → adjust style (light, dark, satellite, streets)
 Map → Map Layers → optional layers (highways, county labels, etc.)

Heatmap and highlight table

Heatmap:
 Required: 2 dimensions, 1+ measure
 Mark type: Square
 Drag dimensions to Rows and Columns
 Drag measure to Color (and optionally Size)
 Square color encodes value

Highlight table:
 Like a regular text table but with conditional cell colors
 Drag dimensions to Rows and Columns
 Drag measure to Text on Marks card
 Drag same measure to Color
 Mark type: Square (NOT Automatic)
 Cells turn into colored boxes with text

Use cases:
 Heatmap: correlation matrices, calendar views, density patterns
 Highlight table: KPI grids where exact values matter and color emphasizes

Treemap and packed bubbles

Treemap:
 Required: 1+ dimension, 1 measure
 Hierarchical rectangles; size = measure value
 Mark type: Square (with no Rows/Columns)
 Drag dimension to Color
 Drag measure to Size

 Best for:
 Showing proportions across many categories
 Hierarchical data (e.g., region → country → city)

Packed bubbles:
 Same idea but circles instead of rectangles
 Mark type: Circle (with no Rows/Columns)
 Dimensions to Color; measures to Size and optionally Label
 
 More playful; less precise
 Useful for high-level overview

Histogram and distribution charts

Histogram:
 Required: 1 continuous measure
 Built using BINS (covered in ch3/s4)

 How:
 Right-click measure in Data pane → Create → Bins
 Set bin size (e.g., $1000 buckets)
 New bin field appears in Data pane
 Drag bin field to Columns (now discrete)
 Drag CNT(any field) or COUNT([Number of Records]) to Rows

Box plot:
 Required: 1 dimension, 1 measure
 Drag dimension to Columns, measure to Rows
 Right-click measure → Disaggregate (or via Analysis menu)
 Analytics pane → drag Box Plot to Cell

 Shows: median (line), quartiles (box), whiskers, outliers

Distribution band:
 Analytics pane → Distribution Band → drag onto axis
 Choose: percentiles, standard deviations, quantiles
 Reference lines for context

Dual-axis chart

Combine two charts on one axis pair (one on top of another)

How:
 Drag two measures to Rows (or Columns)
 Right-click the SECOND measure → Dual Axis
 Tableau shows both with TWO Y-AXES

Synchronize axes (when scales should match):
 Right-click the secondary axis → Synchronize Axis

Different mark types per axis:
 Click each measure in Marks card individually
 Change mark type per axis
 Common: bar + line combo chart

Use cases:
 - Sales (bar) + Profit Margin (line)
 - Temperature + Rainfall
 - Two related KPIs on different scales

Caveat:
 Use synchronized axes when values are comparable
 Use independent axes only with clear labeling — can mislead

Gantt chart

For project tasks, time spans, durations

Required: 1 date dimension, 1 duration measure, optional task name

How:
 Drag Start Date to Columns (continuous)
 Drag Task to Rows
 Mark type: Gantt Bar
 Drag Duration measure to Size

Result:
 Horizontal bars showing each task's span
 Often used for project timelines, employee schedules

Variation:
 Add color for status (In Progress, Complete, Blocked)
 Add reference line for "today"

Text table (crosstab)

Required: 1+ dimensions, 1+ measure

How:
 Drag dimensions to Rows and Columns
 Drag measure to Text on Marks card (or just drag to viz)
 Mark type: Text (auto-selected)

Format:
 Right-click cell → Format → various options
 Conditional formatting via Color on Marks card

When to use:
 Exact numbers required
 Comparing values across categories
 Combined with charts on a dashboard for context

Tableau pros over Excel:
 Built-in filters, sorting, highlighting
 Live data connection
 Easier to publish and share

The Show Me chart types summary

ChartMin requirements
Text table1+ dim, 1+ measure
Heat map2 dim, 1 measure
Highlight table2 dim, 1 measure
Bar chart (vertical)1 dim, 1+ measure
Bar chart (horizontal)1 dim, 1+ measure
Stacked bar2 dim, 1+ measure
Line (discrete)1 date, 1+ measure
Line (continuous)1 date, 1+ measure
Area chart1 date, 1+ measure
Pie1 dim, 1 measure
Scatter2 measures
Bubble1 dim, 1+ measure
Maps (symbol/filled)1 geo field, 0-2 measure
Treemap1+ dim, 1 measure
Histogram1 continuous measure (binned)
Box plot1+ dim, 1 measure (disaggregated)
Gantt1 date, 1+ measure, 1+ dim

Common chart-building mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Pie chart for 10+ categories — use bar or treemap
  2. Bar chart for time series — line is cleaner for continuous time
  3. Line chart with discrete date — gaps look weird; use continuous
  4. Scatter with too many overlapping points — disaggregate carefully or use density
  5. Maps without geographic role assignment — not recognized as locations
  6. Dual axis without synchronization when scales should match — misleading
  7. Stacked bar with too many categories — colors blur together
  8. Highlight table without changing Mark type to Square — colors don't fill cells
  9. Forgetting to disaggregate for scatter (default aggregation gives one point)
  10. Wrong chart for the question — match visual to message
★ ON THE EXAM

"Compare categories?" → Bar chart.

"Trend over time?" → Line chart with continuous date.

"Composition of a whole (few)?" → Pie chart (≤5 slices).

"Composition (many)?" → Treemap or stacked bar.

"Relationship between 2 measures?" → Scatter plot.

"Scatter shows 1 dot?" → Need to disaggregate (Analysis menu).

"Geographic data?" → Map (assign geographic role first).

"Matrix-style table?" → Text table or highlight table.

"Both colored AND has text?" → Highlight table with Mark type Square.

"Distribution?" → Histogram (with bins) or box plot.

"Bar + line combo?" → Dual axis.

"Time spans / project timeline?" → Gantt chart.

"Hierarchical proportions?" → Treemap.

"Multiple lines (one per category)?" → Add dimension to Color on Marks card.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Show Me panel auto-suggests chart types based on selected fields
  • Each chart has minimum requirements (dimensions, measures) shown on hover
  • Bar chart: 1 dim + 1+ measure; horizontal for many categories, vertical for time
  • Line chart: 1 date (continuous) + 1+ measure; add dimension to Color for multiple lines
  • Pie chart: limit to ≤ 5 slices; use treemap for more
  • Scatter plot: 2 measures; disaggregate via Analysis menu for row-level points
  • Maps: require Geographic role assignment; types include filled (choropleth), symbol (bubbles), density
  • Heatmap: 2 dim + 1 measure on Color; Mark type Square
  • Highlight table: text + color in same cell; Mark type must be Square
  • Treemap: hierarchical rectangles sized by measure; no Rows/Columns needed
  • Histogram requires bins (Create → Bins on measure)
  • Box plot: 1 dim + 1 measure, disaggregated; from Analytics pane
  • Dual axis: drag 2 measures to Rows, right-click second → Dual Axis
  • Synchronize Axis when values are comparable
  • Mark type dropdown changes the visual style per sheet

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tableau's grouping features — hierarchies, groups, sets, and bins — let you organize and reshape categorical fields without modifying source data. These are tested on the Specialist exam, especially distinguishing groups from sets (a common confusion).

Hierarchies — drill-down structure

A hierarchy groups related dimensions in a top-down order

Example:
 Country → State → City → Customer
 Year → Quarter → Month → Day (Tableau auto-creates date hierarchies)

Create a hierarchy:
 Data pane → drag one dimension onto another → "Create Hierarchy"
 Name it (e.g., "Geography")
 Reorder by dragging within the hierarchy
 Other dimensions: drag onto the hierarchy to add

Auto-hierarchies:
 Tableau creates Year → Quarter → Month → Day from any date field
 Year icon has a "+" → expand
 Expand or collapse in the Data pane via + / − next to the name

In viz:
 Drag the hierarchy's top level to a shelf
 + button appears next to the pill in shelf
 Click + to drill DOWN one level
 Click − to roll UP one level
 Now your viz drills naturally with one click

Pre-built hierarchies:
 Date hierarchies auto-created
 Geographic role assignments auto-organize

Groups — combining categories

Combine multiple dimension values into a single "group" value

Example:
 Cities: NYC, LA, Chicago → "Tier 1"
 Cities: Boston, Austin → "Tier 2"
 Group becomes a new field in Data pane

Create a group:
 Right-click dimension → Create → Group
 Or: select values in viz/legend → right-click → Group
 Name the group (e.g., "City Tiers")
 Define members in dialog

Use cases:
 Combine duplicates (NYC, New York, N.Y.C. → "New York City")
 Bucket many values into fewer (US states → regions)
 Hide rare values (combine "Other" group)

Edit a group:
 Right-click group field in Data pane → Edit Group
 Add/remove members; rename groups

Visible behavior:
 Same Color/Detail/Filter behaviors as the source dimension
 But each group value covers multiple source values

Include other:
 Check "Include Other" → ungrouped values get an automatic "Other" category

Sets — defining custom subsets

A set is a SUBSET of values from a dimension (either fixed or dynamic)

Two types:

FIXED set:
 Static list of values
 Right-click dimension → Create → Set
 Use General tab → check/uncheck members manually

CONDITION-based set:
 Dynamic; recalculates as data changes
 Condition tab → "By formula" or "By field"
 Example: COUNTD(Orders) > 10
 Members are dimension values where condition holds

TOP set:
 Top N or Bottom N by a measure
 Top tab → Top 10 customers by SUM(Sales)
 Recalculates as filters change

Set properties:
 - IN/OUT field automatically created
 - Drag set to shelf → splits viz into IN vs OUT groups
 - Use in calculations: IF [Customer set] THEN ... 
 - Set membership shown as colored / non-colored marks

Examples:
 "VIP customers" set: top 50 by sales
 "Active campaigns" set: status = "Running"
 "High churn risk" set: complex condition

Multiple sets in viz:
 Combined sets: union, intersection, difference
 Right-click set in Data pane → Create Combined Set

Groups vs Sets — the critical distinction

GroupSet
Combines values into NEW categoriesMarks values as IN or OUT
All groups appear in vizJust IN/OUT or filtered to IN
Fixed membership (manual)Can be dynamic (formula, top N)
Members must be from one fieldSame: from one field
Common use: bucket categoriesCommon use: highlight or filter
Group field replaces in vizSet field adds boolean dimension

Bins — convert measure to categorical

Convert a continuous measure to discrete buckets

Create:
 Right-click measure → Create → Bins
 Choose bin size:
 Tableau suggests a reasonable size based on range
 Override with exact value (e.g., $1000)

Bins become a new dimension field:
 Drag to Columns → each bin becomes a header
 Use with COUNT to build histograms

Adjust bin size:
 Right-click bin field → Edit
 Or use a parameter for dynamic bin size

Histogram with bins:
 Bin field on Columns (discrete)
 CNT(Number of Records) or COUNT([Anything]) on Rows
 Bar chart shows distribution

Use cases:
 Histograms of distributions
 Age groups: 0-9, 10-19, 20-29 from Age measure
 Sales buckets: $0-100, $100-200 from Order Total

Parameters with bins — dynamic histograms

Make bin size a parameter so users can change it:

1. Create parameter "Bin Size" (Number; allowable: 50, 100, 500, 1000)
2. Create bin field on the measure
 Right-click → Create → Bins → "Bin Size" parameter for size
3. Show parameter on viz: right-click parameter → Show Parameter
4. User adjusts → histogram automatically rebuilds

This is a classic Tableau dashboard pattern

Combined sets

Combine two existing sets via:
 Right-click one set → Create Combined Set → pick the other

Operations:
 Union — A OR B
 Intersection — A AND B
 A except B — A and not B
 B except A — B and not A

Use cases:
 - "VIP" set + "Recent buyers" set → intersection = top customers active recently
 - Customers in NY (set) - Customers with complaints (set) = "great NY customers"

Combined sets follow the same IN/OUT pattern
Useful for complex selection logic without writing calc fields

Hierarchical drill-down example

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Date hierarchy drill
// Drag Order Date to Columns
// Tableau auto-creates date hierarchy: YEAR → QUARTER → MONTH → DAY

// Initial view: shows YEAR(Order Date) — bars by year (2022, 2023, 2024)

// Click + on the pill (or pill name "+") → drills to QUARTER
// Now bars are: 2022 Q1, 2022 Q2, ..., 2024 Q4

// Click + again → drills to MONTH
// Now: 2022 Jan, 2022 Feb, ..., 2024 Dec

// Click − to roll back up

// Drill-down in the viz (instead of pill):
// Click a data mark → + appears
// Click + → drills down into THAT bar's children only

// Custom date hierarchy:
// Often the auto Year > Quarter > Month is fine
// But you can build:
// Year > Half > Month for half-year reports
// Year > Fiscal Quarter > Month (custom calendar)

// Geographic hierarchy:
// Right-click Country → Hierarchy → Create Hierarchy
// Drag State, City into it
// Result: drill Country → State → City → Customer with single button

Worked example — sets for highlighting

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Top customers set
// Create dynamic "Top 10 Customers" set
// Right-click Customer Name → Create → Set
// Top tab → By field: Top 10 by SUM(Sales)
// Name: "Top 10 Customers"

// In viz:
// Customer Name on Rows
// SUM(Sales) on Columns
// Top 10 Customers set on Color (Marks card)

// Now: bars color by IN (true) or OUT (false)
// Top 10 customers highlighted in one color; rest in another

// Or: filter to only show set
// Right-click set → "Filter" — only IN members appear
// Equivalent to "filter to top 10 customers"

// Or: use in calculation
// IF [Top 10 Customers] THEN "VIP" ELSE "Other" END
// Build a calculated dimension

// Set updates as data changes
// If new customer enters top 10, set membership updates automatically
// Perfect for dynamic dashboards

Common grouping mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Confusing groups and sets — group combines categories; set marks IN/OUT
  2. Bins too small / too large — over-fragments or hides patterns
  3. Hierarchy with mixed dimensions — only works for natural hierarchies
  4. Forgetting to drag dimension into hierarchy — gets orphaned
  5. Top N set vs Top N filter — set is reusable; filter only narrows the viz
  6. Dynamic set used with non-aggregable expression — formula must work in row context or aggregation
  7. Combined set with overlapping members — verify expected result
  8. Including "Other" without realizing — groups with this option create extra "Other" bucket
  9. Bin parameter forgotten — bin field calculated once, doesn't reflect parameter change
  10. Geographic hierarchy without role assignment — drill-down won't work
★ ON THE EXAM

"Top-down drill structure?" → Hierarchy.

"Combine dimensions into one drill chain?" → Drag one dim onto another → Create Hierarchy.

"Combine values into custom categories?" → Group.

"Mark values as IN or OUT?" → Set.

"Set can be dynamic?" → Yes; via Condition (formula) or Top (Top N).

"Convert measure to discrete buckets?" → Bins.

"Create bin?" → Right-click measure → Create → Bins.

"Bin size from parameter?" → Use parameter as bin size value.

"Combine two sets?" → Combined Set (union, intersection, A-B, B-A).

"Set's IN/OUT field?" → Auto-created when set is dragged to shelf.

"Group includes ungrouped values?" → "Include Other" option.

"Date hierarchy?" → Auto-created on date fields: Year → Quarter → Month → Day.

"Drill down one level?" → Click + on pill or in viz mark.

"Group field replaces dimension?" → Yes; group becomes the visible dimension.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Hierarchies create drill-down paths through related dimensions
  • Date fields auto-create Year → Quarter → Month → Day hierarchy
  • Drag one dimension onto another to create a hierarchy
  • Drill down with + (or up with −) on the pill in a shelf
  • Groups combine multiple dimension values into custom categories
  • "Include Other" option creates an automatic catch-all bucket for ungrouped values
  • Sets mark values as IN or OUT (boolean membership)
  • Sets can be FIXED (manual list), CONDITION-based (formula), or TOP (Top N by measure)
  • Groups change the dimension's display values; sets add a separate IN/OUT field
  • Combine sets via Combined Set: union, intersection, A-B, B-A
  • Bins convert a continuous measure into discrete buckets
  • Bins enable histograms (bin field on Columns, COUNT on Rows)
  • Bin size can be a parameter for interactive control
  • Sets are great for "VIP customer" patterns and dynamic highlighting
  • Groups vs sets is a key exam distinction: categorize vs flag-IN/OUT

Dual-axis rule: synchronize the axes when both measures share the SAME scale/units — otherwise deliberately leave them independent and label clearly, or the chart lies.
