📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Filters are how users (and Tableau) narrow data shown in a viz. There are multiple filter types — dimension, measure, context, top N, table calc — and they fire in a specific order. Filter order affects results. The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam tests filter types and the Order of Operations directly.

Five filter types

TypeFilters by
ExtractLimits what's loaded into extract file
Data sourceApplied at source query level
ContextComputed first; other filters work on context's result
DimensionFilter rows by dimension values
MeasureFilter rows by aggregated measure values
Table calculationFilter using a table calc

The Order of Operations (CRITICAL for exam)

TABLEAU FILTER ORDER
Filters apply in this exact order (top to bottom):

1. Extract filters
2. Data source filters
3. Context filters
4. FIXED LOD expressions
5. Dimension filters
6. INCLUDE / EXCLUDE LOD expressions
7. Measure filters
8. Table calculations
9. Table calculation filters

Understanding this order is essential — it's tested heavily.

Dimension filter

Drag a dimension to the Filters shelf

Filter dialog opens with 4 tabs:
 General — pick specific values (List, Wildcard, Condition, Top)
 Wildcard — match by pattern (starts with, contains, exact match)
 Condition — formula-driven (e.g., "By field" — SUM(Sales) > 1000)
 Top — Top N or Bottom N by a measure

Filter options:
 Show all members (default)
 Include / Exclude selected values
 Use "All" or specific subset

After OK:
 Pill appears on Filters shelf
 Right-click pill → Show Filter to expose as interactive control on viz

Common uses:
 Region = "East"
 Order Date in current year
 Customer Status = "Active"

Show Filter — interactive controls

Right-click filter pill → Show Filter
 Adds the filter as an interactive widget on the right side of viz

Filter widget types (right-click widget → choose):
 Single value (slider) — single date / number
 Single value (dropdown) — pick one
 Single value (list) — radio buttons
 Multiple values (dropdown) — pick many from dropdown
 Multiple values (list) — checkboxes
 Multiple values (custom list) — checkboxes + search
 Wildcard match — text search
 Range of values — date range or number range
 Relative dates — "Last 7 days", "Past 3 months"

Apply to other worksheets:
 Right-click filter widget → Apply to Worksheets:
 Only this worksheet (default)
 All worksheets using this data source
 All using this data source (related)
 Selected worksheets

Filter widgets are key to interactive dashboards.

Measure filter

Drag a measure to Filters shelf

Aggregation choices appear:
 Sum, Average, Median, Count, Min, Max, etc.
 Choose which aggregation to filter on

Filter dialog options:
 Range of values: e.g., SUM(Sales) between 1000 and 50000
 At least: SUM(Sales) >= 1000
 At most: SUM(Sales) <= 5000
 Special: include / exclude null

Note: measure filter operates on AGGREGATED measure
 Different from filtering individual rows (data source filter)
 Different from dimension filter

Use cases:
 Show only regions with SUM(Sales) > $1M
 Hide products with COUNT(Orders) < 10

Context filter — the key concept

A context filter is a regular filter PROMOTED to compute first

Why this matters:
 Top N filter normally uses ALL data
 After context filter, Top N uses only the context's filtered subset

Example without context:
 Region filter: "East" only
 Top 5 Products by Sales filter
 
 Without context: returns top 5 products GLOBALLY (across all regions)
 Then dimension filter restricts to East
 Result: maybe 0-5 East products (whichever are in global top 5)

Example with context:
 Right-click Region filter → "Add to Context"
 Region filter now in context (visible as gray pill)
 Top N runs after context
 Result: top 5 products WITHIN East

How to add to context:
 Right-click any filter pill on Filters shelf → "Add to Context"
 Pill turns gray
 Right-click again → "Remove from Context" to revert

Note: extract and data source filters always behave like context
 Their effects already applied before viz queries

Top N filter

Drag a dimension to Filters → Top tab

Settings:
 By field
 Top / Bottom (radio button)
 N value (e.g., 10)
 By measure (e.g., SUM(Sales))
 Aggregation choice

Result:
 Filter pill on Filters shelf
 Shows only the top N values of the dimension by the chosen measure

Important interactions:
 Top N normally applies AFTER dimension filters
 If you want Top N "within filtered context", add the dimension filter to Context

Example:
 Top 10 Customers by Sales
 Filter to Year 2024
 Without context: Top 10 customers GLOBALLY (multi-year), then keep ones that bought in 2024
 With Year in context: Top 10 customers based on 2024 sales only

Wildcard filter

Drag dimension to Filters → Wildcard tab

Match by pattern:
 Contains
 Starts with
 Ends with
 Exactly matches

Pattern options:
 Match case (checkbox)

Use cases:
 Customer name contains "Inc."
 Product code starts with "ABC-"
 Email ends with "@company.com"

For complex regex-like matching, use Condition tab with CONTAINS()

Condition filter

Drag dimension to Filters → Condition tab

Two options:
 By field:
 Aggregation function on another field
 Example: Region By field SUM(Sales) > 1000000
 Keeps regions where total sales exceed $1M

 By formula:
 Boolean expression
 Example: COUNTD([Orders]) > 50
 Keeps dimension values where condition holds

Use cases:
 Customers who placed > 5 orders
 Products with average rating > 4
 Stores in regions with average sales > target

Filter actions on dashboards

On dashboards, clicking a viz can filter other vizzes
 Covered in detail in ch5/s2 (Dashboard Actions)

Quick setup:
 Click a viz on dashboard → "Use as filter" icon (funnel)
 Now clicking marks in that viz filters other dashboard sheets

This is conceptually a Set Action (since 2018) or Filter Action
Allows users to drive filters interactively

Worked example — top customers in region

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Filter order demo
// Goal: Show top 10 customers BY SALES within currently selected region

// Setup:
// Customer Name on Rows
// SUM(Sales) on Text or Columns
// Region filter (interactive)
// Top 10 Customers filter by SUM(Sales)

// Default behavior (WRONG outcome):
// Top 10 filter applies first (globally)
// Returns top 10 customers across ALL data
// THEN Region filter applied
// Result: only those of the top-10-global who shop in selected region
// (could be 0-10 customers)

// Fix: add Region to context
// Right-click Region filter on Filters shelf → Add to Context
// Region pill turns GRAY (context filter indicator)
// 
// Now order is:
// 1. Region context filter narrows to "East" rows
// 2. Top 10 filter applies to those rows
// Result: top 10 customers WITHIN East — correct!

// Result depends on filter selected
// Always understand the order of operations
// Add filters to context when subsequent filters depend on their result

Common filter mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Forgetting Order of Operations — Top N applies before dimension filters by default
  2. Not using context when Top N should respect another filter
  3. Filter showing wrong values — context filter changes available values
  4. Measure filter behaves like dimension filter — measure filter is post-aggregation
  5. Show Filter doesn't appear — right-click filter pill → Show Filter
  6. Filter applied only to this sheet when wanting all sheets — change Apply to Worksheets scope
  7. Confusing extract filter with data source filter — both restrict data but at different stages
  8. Filter pill greyed out unexpectedly — that's a context filter
  9. Top 10 returns < 10 when global top 10 doesn't match other filters
  10. Table calc filter expected to behave like dimension filter — table calc filter runs last
★ ON THE EXAM

"Filter order critical setting?" → Add to Context (gray pill).

"Top N global vs local?" → Use context filter to make Top N respect prior filters.

"Where do filters live?" → Filters shelf on worksheet.

"Show interactive filter?" → Right-click filter pill → Show Filter.

"Apply to multiple sheets?" → Right-click filter widget → Apply to Worksheets → choose scope.

"Order of operations?" → Extract → Data source → Context → FIXED → Dimension → INCLUDE/EXCLUDE → Measure → Table calc.

"Dimension filter?" → Filter rows by dimension values (e.g., Region = East).

"Measure filter?" → Filter rows by aggregated measure (e.g., SUM(Sales) > 1000).

"Wildcard?" → Pattern matching (contains, starts with, ends with).

"Condition?" → Boolean expression or aggregated value comparison.

"Top N filter?" → Top tab in filter dialog.

"Show only top 5 within filtered set?" → Add other filters to Context.

"Data source filter vs extract filter?" → Data source applies always; extract only during extract refresh.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Filter types: extract, data source, context, dimension, measure, table calculation
  • Order of operations: extract → data source → context → FIXED LOD → dimension → INCLUDE/EXCLUDE → measure → table calc
  • Dimension filters narrow rows by dimension values
  • Measure filters narrow rows by aggregated measure values
  • Context filters compute first, providing a subset for other filters to work on
  • Add a filter to context: right-click pill → "Add to Context" (turns gray)
  • Top N filter normally applies globally; add other filters to context to make Top N local
  • Show Filter: right-click filter pill → enables interactive control on viz
  • Filter widgets: single value, multiple values, wildcard, range, relative dates
  • Apply to Worksheets: choose scope (this only / all with same data source / selected)
  • Wildcard filters match patterns (contains, starts with, ends with, exact)
  • Condition filters use formulas or aggregation comparisons on related fields
  • Extract filters limit data loaded into .hyper extract
  • Data source filters apply at the query level (both live and extract)
  • Table calc filters apply last — after all aggregations and other filters

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Marks card is Tableau's visual encoding control panel — color, size, label, shape, and more. Mastering it lets you pack more information into one chart without clutter. The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam tests recognizing each Marks card slot's behavior.

The Marks card layout

Marks card sits in the middle-left of the workspace

Top section: Mark type dropdown
 Automatic, Bar, Line, Area, Square, Circle, Shape, Text, Map, Pie, Gantt, Polygon, Density

Encoding slots (drag fields to these):
 Color — color encoding (gradient or categorical)
 Size — mark size (continuous or discrete)
 Label — text on the mark
 Detail — disaggregate without showing visually
 Tooltip — what appears on hover
 Path — sequencing (for Line and Polygon)
 Shape — only with Shape mark type
 Angle — only with Pie mark type

Color encoding

Drag a field onto Color:

Dimension (discrete) → categorical color (each value gets a distinct color)
Measure (continuous) → gradient color (low to high)
Multi-field on Color → composite color (rarely useful)

Color palette options:
 Click Color on Marks card → Edit Colors

Categorical palettes (for dimensions):
 - Tableau 10 (default; 10 colors)
 - Color blind (colorblind-safe palette)
 - Seattle Grays (monochrome)
 - Traffic Light (red/yellow/green)
 - Many built-in custom palettes

Sequential palettes (for measures):
 - Blue, Green, Orange, Red gradients
 - Single-color step gradients

Diverging palettes (for measures with a midpoint):
 - Red-White-Green
 - Orange-Blue
 - Useful for variance / +/- values

Custom palette:
 Preferences → my.tableau folder → Preferences.tps file (XML)
 Add palette definitions with hex codes
 Restart Tableau

Color legend:
 Auto-appears at top right; right-click to edit, hide, or filter

Stepped vs gradient color

For measures on Color:

Gradient (default):
 Smooth color transition from low to high
 Best for: continuous values, density

Stepped:
 Discrete bands of color
 Edit Colors → check "Stepped Color" → choose number of steps
 Best for: categorical-feeling buckets ("Low", "Med", "High")

Reversed:
 Edit Colors → "Reverse" checkbox
 Higher values get lower-intensity colors
 Useful when low values = good (e.g., error rates)

Use logarithmic:
 Edit Colors → "Use Log Scale"
 Compresses wide-range values (1 to 1M)

Diverging with center:
 Edit Colors → "Use Full Color Range" or set center value
 Common: red below 0, blue above 0 with white at 0

Size encoding

Drag a measure to Size to encode value through mark area

Bar chart: size affects bar width (less common; uses Rows)
Scatter (Circle): size = circle area
Map (Symbol): size = bubble area
Treemap: size = rectangle area

Range adjustment:
 Click Size on Marks card → slider
 Adjust min and max
 Per mark type (some are bigger by default)

Size legend:
 Right side of viz
 Right-click → format or hide
 Edit min/max marks shown

Caveats:
 Area scales with the SQUARE of dimension; viewers may misjudge
 Use Size in combination with Color and Label for clarity

Label encoding

Drag a field to Label to show text on marks

Common patterns:
 Drag SUM(Sales) to Label → shows the sum on each bar
 Drag Category to Label → shows category name

Label configuration (click Label on Marks card):
 ☑ Show mark labels (toggle on/off)
 Alignment: horizontal/vertical
 Position: Inside end / Outside end / Center / Off
 Marks to label: All / Min/max / Selected only / Highlighted

 Selected marks only:
 Useful for highlighting specific bars (top 5, outliers)
 Click marks in viz to add to label set

Annotations vs labels:
 Annotations (right-click → Annotate → Mark / Point / Area):
 Fixed-text callouts with arrows
 More flexible than labels for storytelling

Quick label formatting:
 Right-click pill in viz → Format → label options
 Change font, color, size

Tooltip encoding

Drag a field to Tooltip to add it to hover info (won't visually encode)

Default tooltip:
 Auto-includes pills already in the viz
 Shows category, value, and detail

Edit tooltip (click Tooltip on Marks card):
 Rich text editor opens
 Insert field references: 
 Format: bold, italic, color, size
 Aggregations: 

Dynamic tooltip example:
  generated  in revenue
 Average order value: 

Insert calculation in tooltip:
 Toolbar in tooltip editor → Insert → choose field

Viz in tooltip:
 Worksheet → "Include in Tooltip" checkbox
 Now this sheet can be embedded as mini-chart in other sheets' tooltips
 Set up in main worksheet: Tooltip → Insert → Sheets → choose
 Result: hover over a bar → mini-chart shows related detail

Detail encoding

Drag a dimension to Detail to DISAGGREGATE the viz without showing visually

Use case:
 Bar chart: SUM(Sales) by Region
 Add Order ID to Detail → instead of one bar per region, see all orders
 Each order is a separate mark, but grouped within region bar

For scatter plots:
 Adding dimensions to Detail creates one point per dimension combination
 Without disaggregating measures explicitly

For maps:
 Add City to Detail → one bubble per city (instead of country totals)

Different from Color:
 Detail: visually identical marks but separately tracked
 Color: same disaggregation + distinct color per value

Useful with Label and Tooltip:
 Detail tracks each record; Label and Tooltip show its info

Shape encoding

Only with Mark type = Shape

Drag a dimension to Shape on Marks card
 Each value gets a distinct shape
 Defaults: filled and open circles, squares, triangles, etc.

Custom shapes:
 Tableau Repository → Shapes folder
 Add custom .png images to a subfolder
 Restart Tableau → custom shapes available in palette

Edit Shape:
 Click Shape → edit per-value assignment
 Map: "Active" → green circle, "Inactive" → red X

Use cases:
 Scatter plot with multiple categories
 Custom symbols for brand consistency
 Custom icons for emphasis

Path and Pages encoding

PATH (only with Line and Polygon mark types):
 Connects marks in a specific order
 Drag a dimension or measure to Path
 
 Use cases:
 - Route on a map (sequenced by time)
 - Polygon vertices (sequenced spatially)

PAGES SHELF (separate from Marks card):
 Drag a dimension to Pages
 Creates an animation: one frame per value
 Playback controls appear

 Use cases:
 - Time animation (year by year)
 - Show progression of a metric
 - Storytelling

Both Path and Pages tend to be intermediate features
 Show Me doesn't auto-suggest them

The marks-card-per-axis trick (dual axis)

In dual-axis charts, EACH AXIS has its own Marks card

Setup:
 Drag two measures to Rows
 Right-click second measure → Dual Axis

Marks card now has tabs at top:
 All — affects both axes simultaneously
 SUM(Sales) — only the first axis's marks
 SUM(Profit) — only the second axis's marks

Use cases:
 Combo chart: bars on one axis, line on the other
 Set Mark type = Bar on first; Line on second
 Each axis gets its own color encoding too

This is what makes dual-axis flexible — independent visual settings

Common Marks card mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using rainbow palette — not colorblind safe; use Color Blind palette
  2. Color for both category and value — confusing if encoding both
  3. Forgetting stepped color for discrete buckets
  4. Size scaling without context — area is square of dimension
  5. Label position default Outside when Inside fits better
  6. No labels on key marks — make readers hover unnecessarily
  7. Default tooltip when custom would be more informative
  8. Detail when Color was meant — Detail doesn't show visually
  9. Shape with too many categories — hard to distinguish shapes
  10. Forgetting marks card tabs in dual axis — settings applied wrong
★ ON THE EXAM

"Encode color?" → Drag field to Color on Marks card.

"Categorical color (each value distinct)?" → Use a dimension on Color.

"Gradient color (low to high)?" → Use a measure on Color.

"Colorblind-safe palette?" → Edit Colors → "Color Blind" palette.

"Stepped color?" → Edit Colors → check "Stepped Color".

"Mark size?" → Drag measure to Size; click Size for range slider.

"Show text on mark?" → Drag field to Label.

"Custom tooltip?" → Click Tooltip → edit text + insert fields.

"Embed mini-chart on hover?" → "Viz in Tooltip" — include sheet in another sheet's tooltip.

"Disaggregate without showing visually?" → Drag dimension to Detail.

"Use custom marker icon?" → Mark type Shape; add PNG to Shapes folder.

"Animation by year?" → Drag field to Pages shelf.

"Each axis own settings in dual axis?" → Marks card tabs (All / axis 1 / axis 2).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Marks card controls visual encoding for the current sheet's mark type
  • Encoding slots: Color, Size, Label, Detail, Tooltip, Path, Shape, Angle (varies by mark type)
  • Color: dimension gives categorical palette; measure gives gradient palette
  • Edit colors via Color → Edit Colors; built-in palettes include Color Blind safe option
  • Stepped Color creates discrete bands instead of a smooth gradient
  • Diverging palettes need a midpoint (often 0)
  • Size encodes magnitude via mark area; adjust min/max with the slider
  • Label encodes a value as text; configure position, alignment, and which marks
  • Tooltip lets you add fields to the hover popup with rich text + inserted refs
  • Viz in Tooltip embeds a mini-chart from another sheet on hover
  • Detail disaggregates marks without visual encoding — useful for granularity
  • Shape (only with Mark type Shape) assigns custom markers to dimension values
  • Path orders marks for line/polygon connections
  • Pages shelf creates an animation across a dimension's values
  • Dual axis: Marks card has tabs per axis; each can have its own mark type and encoding

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When drag-and-drop runs out, calculated fields are how you express custom logic in Tableau. They're written in Tableau's calculation language (similar to SQL/Excel) and create reusable derived fields. The Specialist exam tests recognizing function categories and common patterns.

Creating a calculated field

Three ways:
 1. Data pane → right-click → Create Calculated Field
 2. Analysis menu → Create Calculated Field
 3. Right-click in shelf → Create Calculated Field

Calculation editor opens:
 Top: name your field
 Middle: write the formula
 Bottom: list of functions; click to insert
 Right side: documentation for the highlighted function

Save with green "Calculation is valid" indicator
Red error message guides what's wrong

Field appears in Data pane with "=" prefix icon
Use like any other field: drag to shelves, color, filter

Three calculation types

TypeEvaluates atExample
Row-level (basic)Each underlying data row[Revenue] - [Cost]
AggregateAfter groupingSUM([Revenue]) - SUM([Cost])
LOD (Level of Detail)Specific grain regardless of viz{FIXED [Customer] : SUM([Sales])}

You cannot mix row-level and aggregate in the same expression (Tableau errors out). Either all-row-level or all-aggregate inside a calc.

Logical functions

IF / THEN / ELSE / END
 IF [Profit] > 0 THEN "Profitable" ELSE "Loss" END

IF / ELSEIF / END
 IF [Sales] > 10000 THEN "High"
 ELSEIF [Sales] > 1000 THEN "Medium"
 ELSE "Low"
 END

IIF (inline conditional)
 IIF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false, value_if_unknown)
 IIF([Status] = "Active", 1, 0)

CASE / WHEN / THEN / END
 CASE [Region]
 WHEN "East" THEN "EMEA"
 WHEN "West" THEN "Americas"
 ELSE "Other"
 END

 CASE is simpler than IF for value matching
 But CASE compares to a SINGLE value; IF can handle complex conditions

ISNULL, IFNULL, ZN
 ISNULL([Region]) — returns true if NULL
 IFNULL([Region], "?") — replace null with default
 ZN([Sales]) — null → 0

Boolean operators:
 AND, OR, NOT
 Example: IF [Region] = "East" AND [Sales] > 1000 THEN ... END

String functions

LEN(s) — length of string
LEFT(s, n) — first N characters
RIGHT(s, n) — last N characters
MID(s, start, n) — substring from position
UPPER(s) — all caps
LOWER(s) — all lowercase
PROPER(s) — Title Case

TRIM(s) — remove leading/trailing whitespace
LTRIM(s), RTRIM(s) — trim left or right only

CONTAINS(s, substring)
STARTSWITH(s, substring)
ENDSWITH(s, substring)
FIND(s, substring, [start]) — position of substring

REPLACE(s, old, new)
SPLIT(s, delimiter, position)

Examples:
 Full Name = [First Name] + " " + [Last Name]
 Domain = SPLIT([Email], "@", 2)
 Initials = LEFT([First Name], 1) + LEFT([Last Name], 1)
 IsCorporate = ENDSWITH([Email], "@company.com")

Date functions

TODAY() — current date
NOW() — current datetime

YEAR(date), MONTH(date), DAY(date), WEEK(date)
DATEPART('year', [date]) — extract part
DATETRUNC('month', [date]) — truncate to month start
DATENAME('month', [date]) — month name as string ("January")

DATEADD('day', 7, [date]) — add 7 days
DATEDIFF('day', start, end) — difference in days
 Units: year, quarter, month, week, day, hour, minute, second

DATEPARSE(format, string) — parse string to date
 Example: DATEPARSE("yyyy-MM-dd", "2024-01-15")

MAKEDATE(year, month, day) — build a date

Common patterns:
 Days since order = DATEDIFF('day', [Order Date], TODAY())
 Is current year = YEAR([Order Date]) = YEAR(TODAY())
 Quarter label = "Q" + STR(DATEPART('quarter', [date])) + " " + STR(YEAR([date]))

Number functions

ROUND([x], digits)
CEILING([x]), FLOOR([x])
ABS([x])
SIGN([x]) — returns 1, 0, or -1
POWER([x], 2) — x squared
SQRT([x])
EXP([x]), LN([x]), LOG([x], base)

MIN(a, b) — minimum of two values
MAX(a, b) — maximum of two values

MOD([x], divisor) — modulo

Aggregations (with measure):
 SUM, AVG, MEDIAN, MIN, MAX
 COUNT, COUNTD (count distinct)
 STDEV, STDEVP, VAR, VARP
 PERCENTILE([Sales], 0.95)

Type conversion functions

STR([number]) — convert to string
INT([float]) — to integer (truncates)
FLOAT([string]) — to float
DATE([datetime]) — date only
DATETIME([date]) — date with 00:00 time
BOOL([0_or_1]) — to boolean

Common need:
 Concatenating in tooltip → STR(SUM([Sales]))
 Parsing IDs → INT([ID String])

Implicit vs explicit conversion:
 Most operators auto-convert where reasonable
 But concatenation with + on strings requires explicit STR()

Aggregate functions

Used in measures and aggregate calculations

SUM, AVG, MEDIAN, MIN, MAX
COUNT, COUNTD (count distinct)
STDEV, STDEVP (population)
VAR, VARP (population)
PERCENTILE([field], 0.5)

ATTR([dimension]) — used for blending; returns value if unique, * otherwise

Example aggregate calc:
 Profit Ratio = SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Revenue])
 Customer Count = COUNTD([Customer ID])

You can't mix:
 Row level: [Profit] / [Revenue]
 Aggregate: SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Revenue])
 These give different results for non-equal-weight data

NULL handling

ISNULL([Field]) — returns true if value is null
IFNULL([Field], default) — replace null with default
ZN([Field]) — null → 0 (numeric only)

When NULL propagates:
 Math: anything + NULL = NULL
 String: anything + NULL = NULL
 Boolean: NULL AND TRUE = NULL (not FALSE)

Aggregates and nulls:
 SUM, AVG, COUNT ignore NULL by default
 COUNTD ignores NULL
 ATTR returns "*" if values vary OR null + non-null mix

Best practice:
 Use IFNULL or ZN at the start of calculations
 Avoid surprises in dashboards

Common calculated field patterns

// Profit / Loss flag
Profitability = IF [Profit] > 0 THEN "Profitable" ELSE "Loss" END

// Discount percentage
Discount_Pct = ([List Price] - [Sale Price]) / [List Price]

// Customer lifetime value bucket
LTV_Bucket =
 IF [LTV] >= 10000 THEN "VIP"
 ELSEIF [LTV] >= 5000 THEN "High"
 ELSEIF [LTV] >= 1000 THEN "Medium"
 ELSE "Low"
 END

// Age group from birth date
Age_Group =
 IF DATEDIFF('year', [DOB], TODAY()) < 18 THEN "Minor"
 ELSEIF DATEDIFF('year', [DOB], TODAY()) < 65 THEN "Adult"
 ELSE "Senior"
 END

// Year-month label
YearMonth = DATENAME('month', [Order Date]) + " " + STR(YEAR([Order Date]))

// Current vs previous year flag
Is_Current_Year = YEAR([Order Date]) = YEAR(TODAY())

// Aggregate margin
Profit_Margin = SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Revenue])

// Safe divide
Safe_Margin = IIF(SUM([Revenue]) = 0, NULL, SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Revenue]))

Worked example — customer segmentation

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Build customer segment field
// Goal: classify customers into segments based on total spend and recency

// Field 1: Total Spend Per Customer (row-level helper)
// This is a LOD; placeholder for now (covered in s2)
Total_Customer_Spend = {FIXED [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])}

// Field 2: Last Order Per Customer (LOD)
Last_Order_Date = {FIXED [Customer ID] : MAX([Order Date])}

// Field 3: Days Since Last Order
Days_Since_Last_Order = DATEDIFF('day', [Last_Order_Date], TODAY())

// Field 4: Customer Segment (the final categorization)
Customer_Segment =
 IF [Total_Customer_Spend] >= 10000 AND [Days_Since_Last_Order] <= 90
 THEN "Active VIP"
 ELSEIF [Total_Customer_Spend] >= 10000
 THEN "Lapsed VIP"
 ELSEIF [Total_Customer_Spend] >= 1000 AND [Days_Since_Last_Order] <= 90
 THEN "Active Regular"
 ELSEIF [Total_Customer_Spend] >= 1000
 THEN "Lapsed Regular"
 ELSE
 "Low Value"
 END

// Now drag Customer_Segment to viz: bar chart of segment counts
// Use it for color encoding, filtering, drill-through

// Field 5: Tooltip-ready summary
Segment_Summary =
 STR(COUNTD([Customer ID])) + " customers in " + [Customer_Segment]
 + " (avg spend: $" + STR(ROUND(AVG([Total_Customer_Spend]), 0)) + ")"

Calculated field editor tips

Comments:
 // Single line comment
 /* Multi-line
 comment */

Formatting:
 Use indentation for readability
 Break long IFs across multiple lines
 Add blank lines between logical sections

Function help:
 Right side of editor shows the highlighted function's signature
 Examples included for most functions

Drag fields into the formula:
 Click and drag from Data pane
 Tableau wraps with [Square Brackets] automatically

Insert function:
 Click function in list (bottom right) → inserts at cursor

Save and reuse:
 Calculated fields belong to the workbook
 Copy to another workbook: copy formula text
 Save as Tableau Data Source (.tds) to share with model

Common calculated field mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Mixing row-level and aggregate — Tableau errors; pick one approach
  2. Forgetting END in IF/CASE statements
  3. Using = for assignment — Tableau uses = for comparison; you don't "assign" in formulas
  4. NULL propagation in math — wrap with IFNULL/ZN
  5. String concatenation without STR() — STR(SUM([Sales])), not just SUM
  6. Date difference vs date arithmetic confusion — DATEDIFF returns INT
  7. Incorrect aggregation in ratios — row-level vs aggregate differ on averages
  8. Calling DATEPART without quotes around 'year' — first arg is a string literal
  9. Forgetting that boolean fields can be NULL too — three-state logic
  10. Calculation marked aggregate but used as dimension — green vs blue confusion
★ ON THE EXAM

"Create calculated field?" → Right-click in Data pane → Create Calculated Field.

"Row-level calc?" → Operates on each underlying row.

"Aggregate calc?" → Operates after grouping; uses SUM, AVG, etc.

"Mix row-level + aggregate?" → Not allowed; Tableau errors.

"Multiple conditions?" → IF/ELSEIF/END or CASE.

"Replace null with 0?" → ZN([field]).

"Replace null with default?" → IFNULL([field], default).

"Concatenate string + number?" → Use STR() to convert.

"Days between dates?" → DATEDIFF('day', start, end).

"Add 30 days?" → DATEADD('day', 30, [date]).

"Substring?" → MID, LEFT, RIGHT, or SPLIT.

"Test for null?" → ISNULL([field]).

"Count distinct?" → COUNTD([field]).

"= comparison vs assignment?" → = is comparison only; no assignment in formulas.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Calculated fields are reusable derived fields you create in the calculation editor
  • Three types: row-level, aggregate, and LOD (Level of Detail)
  • Cannot mix row-level and aggregate in the same expression
  • Logical functions: IF/THEN/ELSE/END, IF/ELSEIF, IIF, CASE/WHEN
  • Null handling: ISNULL, IFNULL, ZN (replace null with 0)
  • String functions: LEN, LEFT/RIGHT/MID, UPPER/LOWER/PROPER, CONTAINS, SPLIT
  • Date functions: TODAY/NOW, YEAR/MONTH/DAY, DATEPART, DATETRUNC, DATEADD, DATEDIFF
  • Number functions: ROUND, FLOOR, CEILING, ABS, POWER, SQRT
  • Type conversion: STR, INT, FLOAT, DATE, DATETIME, BOOL
  • Aggregate functions: SUM, AVG, MEDIAN, COUNT, COUNTD, STDEV, PERCENTILE
  • String concatenation: use + between strings; convert numbers with STR()
  • Add comments with // (single-line) or /* */ (multi-line)
  • Tableau auto-wraps field references in [Square Brackets]
  • Calculated fields appear in Data pane with an "=" icon
  • Use the function list at bottom of editor for syntax help

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
FIXEDIgnores viz; uses ONLY specified dimensions
INCLUDEAdds the specified dimensions to viz's grain
EXCLUDERemoves the specified dimensions from viz's grain
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

LOD (Level of Detail) expressions are the most powerful — and most exam-tested — feature in Tableau calculations. They let you compute at a DIFFERENT GRAIN than the viz uses. The Specialist exam tests FIXED, INCLUDE, EXCLUDE distinctions.

The level-of-detail problem

THE GRAIN PROBLEM
Every viz has a "viz level of detail" set by the dimensions on shelves.

By default, aggregations work at the VIZ grain.
Sometimes you need to aggregate at a DIFFERENT grain.

Examples:
  Show profit per region but as % of company-wide total → company grain
  Show each order with that customer's total lifetime spend → customer grain
  Show daily sales with monthly target as reference → month grain

LOD expressions let you choose the grain.

Three LOD types

TypeBehaviorSyntax
FIXEDIgnores viz; uses ONLY specified dimensions{FIXED [Customer] : SUM([Sales])}
INCLUDEAdds the specified dimensions to viz's grain{INCLUDE [Product] : SUM([Sales])}
EXCLUDERemoves the specified dimensions from viz's grain{EXCLUDE [Region] : SUM([Sales])}

FIXED — the most common LOD

{FIXED [dim1], [dim2], ... : aggregation}

IGNORES the viz's dimensions; uses ONLY what's inside the FIXED clause

Example 1: Customer lifetime value
 {FIXED [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])}
 
 In a viz showing orders by date:
 Each row (order) gets the SAME LTV value
 The total for that customer is repeated on each of their orders
 
Example 2: Company-wide total (no dimensions specified)
 {FIXED : SUM([Sales])}
 
 Returns the grand total
 Useful for "% of total" calculations

Example 3: Region totals regardless of filters
 {FIXED [Region] : SUM([Sales])}
 
 Each region's total stays constant even as other filters narrow the data
 Note: respects context filters but NOT regular dimension filters

Common patterns:
 Days since first order = DATEDIFF('day', 
 {FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Order Date])}, 
 TODAY())
 
 First order amount = {FIXED [Customer] : 
 MIN(IIF([Order Date] = {FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Order Date])}, [Sales], NULL))}

INCLUDE — augment viz grain

{INCLUDE [dim] : aggregation}

ADDS the specified dimension to the viz's grain BEFORE aggregating
 Then aggregates UP to the viz grain

Example:
 Viz: SUM(Sales) by Region
 
 Average Customer Sales per Region:
 {INCLUDE [Customer] : SUM([Sales])}
 
 Tableau computes: customer-level totals
 For each customer-region, sum of sales
 
 Then aggregates at region level:
 AVG({INCLUDE [Customer] : SUM([Sales])})
 
 Result: "average customer total spend per region"
 Without INCLUDE: AVG([Sales]) would average individual orders, not customers

Use cases:
 Compute per-customer/per-product metrics, then aggregate to viz level
 Often wrapped in another aggregation: AVG, MIN, MAX

EXCLUDE — remove viz dimensions

{EXCLUDE [dim] : aggregation}

REMOVES the specified dimension from viz's grain
 Aggregates "wider" than the viz

Example:
 Viz: SUM(Sales) by Region by Product
 
 Region total (ignoring product):
 {EXCLUDE [Product] : SUM([Sales])}
 
 Returns total sales for region regardless of which product the row represents
 
 % of region:
 SUM([Sales]) / {EXCLUDE [Product] : SUM([Sales])}

Common use cases:
 % of category total (drop Product from viz grain)
 Difference from average (drop the specific row's dimension)
 Comparative metrics

FIXED vs INCLUDE — the key difference

FIXED ignores viz dimensions entirely
INCLUDE adds to them

Example viz: Region on Rows, Product on Columns

FIXED Region:
 {FIXED [Region] : SUM([Sales])}
 Returns: regional total, ignoring Product
 Per row: same value regardless of Product column

INCLUDE Customer (where Customer not in viz):
 {INCLUDE [Customer] : SUM([Sales])}
 Returns: rolls up to per-customer first, then to viz grain (Region × Product)
 Average gives: AVG({INCLUDE [Customer] : SUM([Sales])})

EXCLUDE Product (where Product is in viz):
 {EXCLUDE [Product] : SUM([Sales])}
 Returns: rolls up to just Region level
 Useful: each Product cell shows the Region total (denominator for % calc)

Order of Operations and LODs

★ WHEN LODS FIRE

From the Order of Operations:

  1. Extract filters
  2. Data source filters
  3. Context filters
  4. FIXED LODs ← compute here
  5. Dimension filters
  6. INCLUDE / EXCLUDE LODs ← compute here
  7. Measure filters
  8. Table calculations

Implications:

  • FIXED ignores dimension filters; ONLY context filters affect FIXED
  • To make a FIXED respect a dimension filter, add the filter to Context
  • INCLUDE / EXCLUDE respect dimension filters by default

LOD use cases (canonical patterns)

1. Percent of total

% of total = SUM([Sales]) / {FIXED : SUM([Sales])}

 Denominator is grand total regardless of filters
 
 Or respecting filters:
 % of filtered total = SUM([Sales]) / {EXCLUDE [current dim] : SUM([Sales])}

2. Customer order count and segmentation

Customer Order Count = {FIXED [Customer ID] : COUNTD([Order ID])}

Customer Segment =
 IF [Customer Order Count] >= 10 THEN "Loyal"
 ELSEIF [Customer Order Count] >= 3 THEN "Repeat"
 ELSE "One-time"
 END

Now drag Customer Segment to any viz — uses correct customer-level metric

3. Date of first / last order

First Order Date = {FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Order Date])}
Last Order Date = {FIXED [Customer] : MAX([Order Date])}

Days Active = DATEDIFF('day', [First Order Date], [Last Order Date])
Customer Lifetime (years) = DATEDIFF('year', [First Order Date], TODAY())

4. Cohort analysis

Acquisition Cohort = DATETRUNC('month', {FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Order Date])})

 All orders from a customer get the SAME cohort value
 Drag Cohort to rows, time period to columns → cohort retention chart

5. Pareto / contribution analysis

% of company total = 
 SUM([Sales]) / {FIXED : SUM([Sales])}

% of region total (when region in viz) =
 SUM([Sales]) / SUM({EXCLUDE [Product] : SUM([Sales])})

Top 20% concentration:
 Use Bins on customers ranked by spend → see Pareto curve

Worked example — RFM segmentation

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary)
// Build customer RFM segments using LODs

// Recency: days since last order
Recency = DATEDIFF('day',
 {FIXED [Customer ID] : MAX([Order Date])},
 TODAY())

// Frequency: total number of distinct orders per customer
Frequency = {FIXED [Customer ID] : COUNTD([Order ID])}

// Monetary: total spend per customer
Monetary = {FIXED [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])}

// R score: 1 (worst, oldest) to 5 (best, recent)
R_Score =
 IF [Recency] <= 30 THEN 5
 ELSEIF [Recency] <= 90 THEN 4
 ELSEIF [Recency] <= 180 THEN 3
 ELSEIF [Recency] <= 365 THEN 2
 ELSE 1
 END

// F and M scores: 1-5 quintiles using thresholds
F_Score =
 IF [Frequency] >= 20 THEN 5
 ELSEIF [Frequency] >= 10 THEN 4
 ELSEIF [Frequency] >= 5 THEN 3
 ELSEIF [Frequency] >= 2 THEN 2
 ELSE 1
 END

M_Score =
 IF [Monetary] >= 10000 THEN 5
 ELSEIF [Monetary] >= 5000 THEN 4
 ELSEIF [Monetary] >= 1000 THEN 3
 ELSEIF [Monetary] >= 100 THEN 2
 ELSE 1
 END

// Final segment label
RFM_Segment =
 IF [R_Score] >= 4 AND [F_Score] >= 4 AND [M_Score] >= 4
 THEN "Champions"
 ELSEIF [R_Score] >= 3 AND [F_Score] >= 3
 THEN "Loyal Customers"
 ELSEIF [R_Score] >= 4 AND [F_Score] <= 2
 THEN "New Customers"
 ELSEIF [R_Score] <= 2 AND [F_Score] >= 3
 THEN "At Risk"
 ELSEIF [R_Score] <= 2 AND [M_Score] >= 4
 THEN "Cannot Lose Them"
 ELSE
 "Other"
 END

// Now build:
// Bar chart: COUNTD([Customer ID]) by RFM_Segment
// Bubble chart: Frequency vs Monetary; size = Recency
// Each viz uses customer-level RFM values regardless of viz grain

Performance considerations

FIXED LODs query at the FIXED grain (could be very small or very large)
 Many FIXEDs in one viz: each adds a query
 Cache them: use one FIXED with multiple aggregations if possible

INCLUDE / EXCLUDE compute in-flight; faster but less reusable

Best practices:
 - Use LODs in dimensions or as part of calculated fields, not raw in every viz
 - Materialize commonly used LODs as separate fields
 - When possible, prefer FIXED for reusable computations

Common LOD mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. FIXED ignores dimension filters — totals don't respond to selections; add filter to context
  2. INCLUDE without outer aggregation — Tableau wants AVG/MIN/MAX/SUM wrapping it
  3. EXCLUDE on dimension NOT in viz — no effect
  4. Confusing FIXED with INCLUDE — FIXED ignores viz; INCLUDE adds to it
  5. FIXED grand total {FIXED : ...} — leaving colon makes no-dimension expression
  6. LODs in dimension filter formulas — order issues; not all combinations valid
  7. Forgetting LOD applies before measure filter — affects results visibly
  8. Performance: too many FIXED in one workbook — bloats queries
  9. FIXED + null result — when no rows match, can be unexpected
  10. Misusing INCLUDE/EXCLUDE order of operations — they fire AFTER dimension filters
★ ON THE EXAM

"LOD syntax?" → {FIXED|INCLUDE|EXCLUDE [dims] : aggregation}.

"Compute at customer level regardless of viz?" → FIXED.

"Add a dimension to the viz grain temporarily?" → INCLUDE.

"Remove a dimension from viz grain?" → EXCLUDE.

"FIXED respects what filters?" → Context filters only (and source/extract).

"INCLUDE / EXCLUDE respect what filters?" → Context AND dimension filters.

"Grand total?" → {FIXED : SUM([Sales])} (no dim before colon).

"Customer LTV?" → {FIXED [Customer] : SUM([Sales])}.

"% of total?" → SUM(Sales) / {FIXED : SUM(Sales)}.

"Make FIXED respect filter?" → Add filter to Context.

"FIXED in Order of Operations?" → Before dimension filters; after context filters.

"INCLUDE outer aggregation?" → Usually wrapped in AVG/MIN/MAX/SUM.

"First order date per customer?" → {FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Order Date])}.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • LOD expressions compute at a grain DIFFERENT from the viz
  • Three types: FIXED (ignore viz), INCLUDE (add to viz grain), EXCLUDE (remove from viz grain)
  • Syntax: {FIXED|INCLUDE|EXCLUDE [dims] : aggregation}
  • FIXED uses only the specified dimensions, ignoring viz
  • INCLUDE adds the specified dimensions to the viz's grain before aggregating
  • EXCLUDE removes the specified dimensions from the viz's grain
  • FIXED with no dimensions = grand total: {FIXED : SUM([Sales])}
  • FIXED LODs respect only context and source/extract filters — not dimension filters
  • INCLUDE/EXCLUDE respect both context AND dimension filters
  • Add dimension filters to Context to make FIXED respect them
  • Common pattern: customer LTV = {FIXED [Customer] : SUM([Sales])}
  • Pareto / % of total: SUM([Sales]) / {FIXED : SUM([Sales])}
  • Cohort: {FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Order Date])}
  • INCLUDE typically wrapped in outer aggregation (AVG, MIN, MAX)
  • Order of operations places FIXED before dimension filters; INCLUDE/EXCLUDE after

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Table calculations compute on the data ALREADY in the viz — running totals, year-over-year change, ranks, percent of column. They're computed CLIENT-SIDE after the query returns. The Specialist exam tests recognizing table calc patterns and partitioning concepts.

What table calculations are

TABLE CALCS
Table calculations operate on the DATA ALREADY IN THE VIZ.
They're computed AFTER aggregation, on the rendered table of values.

Key contrast:
  Regular calc / LOD: queries the data source
  Table calc: computes locally from displayed values

This is why table calcs depend on the viz's structure — they can shift between rows, sum across columns, etc.

Quick table calcs from right-click

Right-click a measure pill on a shelf → "Quick Table Calculation":

 Running Total — cumulative sum from start
 Difference — diff from previous value
 Percent Difference — % change from previous
 Percent of Total — share of total
 Rank — rank by value
 Percentile — percentile rank
 Moving Average — rolling N-period average
 YTD Total — year-to-date sum
 Compound Growth Rate — geometric growth rate
 Year over Year Growth — % change vs same period last year
 YTD Growth — YTD vs YTD last year

After applying:
 Pill gets a Δ triangle indicator
 Right-click again → Edit Table Calculation for advanced options

Custom table calculations

Create Calculated Field → use table calc functions:

WINDOW_SUM(expression, [start, end])
WINDOW_AVG(expression)
WINDOW_MIN, WINDOW_MAX, WINDOW_MEDIAN
WINDOW_COUNT, WINDOW_VAR, WINDOW_STDEV

RUNNING_SUM(expression)
RUNNING_AVG, RUNNING_MIN, RUNNING_MAX, RUNNING_COUNT

PREVIOUS_VALUE(default) — value from previous mark
LOOKUP(expression, offset) — value from N positions away (negative or positive)
FIRST() — offset to first mark in partition
LAST() — offset to last mark
INDEX() — current row's position (1-based)
SIZE() — total marks in partition

RANK(expression)
RANK_DENSE, RANK_MODIFIED, RANK_UNIQUE
RANK_PERCENTILE

TOTAL(expression) — sum across whole partition

SCRIPT_REAL, SCRIPT_STR — call external scripts (Python/R)

The most important concept: addressing and partitioning

ADDRESSING vs PARTITIONING
Every table calc has two roles:

Addressing fields: the dimension the calc moves ALONG
  Direction of computation (e.g., "across columns" or "down rows")

Partitioning fields: the dimensions that define SEPARATE groups
  Restart the calc within each group

Example: running total across months (addressing = Month), restarts per Year (partitioning = Year) 
Configure via:
 Right-click table calc pill → Edit Table Calculation
 
 "Compute using" options:
 Table (across) — left to right
 Table (down) — top to bottom
 Table (across then down) — wraps
 Table (down then across) — wraps
 Pane (across / down) — within each pane
 Cell — single cell only
 Specific Dimensions... — pick exactly which dims address vs partition

Specific Dimensions:
 Drag dimensions between "addressing" and "partitioning"
 Most control; harder to get right
 Click "Show calculation assistant" to see effect visually

Common table calc patterns

Running total

Right-click SUM(Sales) → Quick Table Calculation → Running Total

Or custom: RUNNING_SUM(SUM([Sales]))

Compute using: 
 - Table (across) if Date on Columns
 - Table (down) if Date on Rows

To reset per year:
 Edit Table Calculation → Specific Dimensions
 Address Month; partition Year

Year-over-year growth

Right-click SUM(Sales) → Quick Table Calculation → Year over Year Growth

Manual:
 YoY % = (ZN(SUM([Sales])) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1)) / 
 ABS(LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1))

Where -1 means "value from one period earlier"

Percent of total

Right-click SUM(Sales) → Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total

Or custom: SUM([Sales]) / TOTAL(SUM([Sales]))

By default, % of total across the row OR down the column
 Configure direction in Edit Table Calc

Rank

Right-click SUM(Sales) → Rank

Variants:
 RANK — competition rank (1, 2, 2, 4)
 RANK_DENSE — gapless (1, 2, 2, 3)
 RANK_MODIFIED — opposite of competition (1, 3, 3, 4)
 RANK_UNIQUE — every value unique (1, 2, 3, 4)
 RANK_PERCENTILE — 0-1 percentile

Useful: RANK_UNIQUE for "Top N" patterns without ties

Moving average

Right-click SUM(Sales) → Moving Average

Default: 2 previous values + current = 3-period average
Edit to change window size and offset

Custom: WINDOW_AVG(SUM([Sales]), -2, 0)
 -2 = 2 marks before
 0 = current mark
 Range: -2 to 0 inclusive = 3 marks

Edit Table Calculation dialog

Click "Δ" triangle on pill → Edit Table Calculation

Options vary by table calc type:

Difference:
 Relative to: previous, next, first, last, specific value
 
Running:
 Function: sum, avg, min, max, count
 Restart every: dimension boundary (for reset behavior)
 
Window:
 Window of -2 to 0 (default for 3-period moving)
 Or other ranges
 
Compute using:
 Choose how the table calc walks through the viz
 Use predefined directions or Specific Dimensions

Test with the on-screen preview
Shows arrows indicating direction of compute

Filter actions and table calcs

⚠ TABLE CALC FILTERS

Filtering on a table calc is DIFFERENT from a regular filter:

  • Table calc filters apply LAST (after the table calc runs)
  • This means table calc values won't recompute after filter
  • Example: "Show only top 5 ranked products"
  • RANK computes first; then filter hides ranks > 5
  • Useful when you want true rank values to stay stable

Worked example — year-over-year trend

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sales with YoY growth
// Goal: chart with Sales line and YoY growth % overlay

// Setup:
// MONTH(Order Date) on Columns (Continuous Date Value)
// SUM(Sales) on Rows
// Year(Order Date) on Detail
//
// Default view: one line per year showing monthly trend

// Add YoY growth as table calc:
// Drag SUM(Sales) to Rows AGAIN (creates second axis)
// Right-click second pill → Quick Table Calculation → Year over Year Growth
// Pill gets Δ triangle and shows YoY %
// Edit Table Calc → "Compute using" → Year(Order Date)

// Configure dual axis:
// Right-click YoY axis → Dual Axis
// Synchronize Axis (right-click second axis) — only if values comparable; usually NOT here
// Marks card: Sales line + YoY bars

// Final viz:
// Each month shows total Sales (line) and YoY change (bars)
// Clear visual of when growth was positive vs negative

// Alternative: built-in YoY trick
// Right-click YEAR(Date) pill → Show Header
// Add "Year over Year Growth" quick table calc to SUM(Sales)
// No need for dual axis

Table calcs vs LODs — when to use each

Table CalcLOD
Operates on viz outputOperates on data source
Computes locally (after query)Computed by DB at query time
Depends on viz structureIndependent of viz
Use for: running totals, YoY, ranks, moving avgUse for: customer-level totals, % of grand total
Slower for very large dataGenerally faster for big data

Table calc functions reference

NAVIGATION (within partition):
 FIRST() — offset to first mark (negative number)
 LAST() — offset to last mark
 INDEX() — current 1-based index
 SIZE() — total number of marks
 LOOKUP(expr, offset) — value at offset away from current

AGGREGATES:
 WINDOW_SUM, WINDOW_AVG, WINDOW_MIN, WINDOW_MAX, WINDOW_MEDIAN
 WINDOW_COUNT, WINDOW_VAR, WINDOW_STDEV
 TOTAL(expr) — sum across whole partition

RUNNING:
 RUNNING_SUM(expr)
 RUNNING_AVG, RUNNING_MIN, RUNNING_MAX, RUNNING_COUNT

DIFFERENCE:
 Previous value: LOOKUP(expr, -1)
 Difference: expr - LOOKUP(expr, -1)
 Pct difference: (expr - LOOKUP(expr, -1)) / LOOKUP(expr, -1)

RANKING:
 RANK(expr, [asc/desc])
 RANK_DENSE, RANK_MODIFIED, RANK_UNIQUE
 RANK_PERCENTILE

SPECIAL:
 PREVIOUS_VALUE(default) — value computed previously
 SCRIPT_* — external scripts (Python/R)
 WINDOW_CORR, WINDOW_COVAR — correlation/covariance

Common table calc mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Wrong "compute using" direction — running total goes wrong way
  2. Forgetting to partition correctly — YoY doesn't reset per year
  3. Confusing addressing and partitioning — they're inverse
  4. Table calc filter applied wrong — fires after calc; not before
  5. Hardcoded direction breaks when viz layout changes
  6. Using table calc when LOD would be cleaner — and vice versa
  7. Forgetting Δ triangle indicator — easy to overlook
  8. Running total doesn't reset — partition by appropriate dim
  9. Rank shows wrong order — check asc/desc parameter
  10. Filtering on table calc result — use it for "show top N" but don't expect ranks to renumber
★ ON THE EXAM

"Computes after data query?" → Table calculation.

"Quick table calc?" → Right-click measure pill → Quick Table Calculation.

"Custom table calc?" → Use WINDOW_*, RUNNING_*, LOOKUP, RANK, INDEX, SIZE functions.

"Addressing fields?" → The dimension the calc moves ALONG.

"Partitioning fields?" → Dimensions defining separate groups (restart per).

"Compute using?" → How the table calc walks the viz; configurable.

"Running total?" → Quick Table Calc or RUNNING_SUM().

"YoY growth?" → Quick Table Calc → Year over Year Growth.

"Previous value?" → LOOKUP(expr, -1).

"Rank within partition?" → RANK(SUM([Sales])); set Compute using to partition dim.

"Rank with no ties?" → RANK_UNIQUE.

"Moving average?" → WINDOW_AVG(SUM([Sales]), -2, 0).

"% of total?" → SUM(Sales) / TOTAL(SUM(Sales)).

"Table calc filter applies?" → AFTER the table calc — last in Order of Operations.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Table calculations compute on the viz's data AFTER aggregation — client-side
  • Quick Table Calculations: right-click measure → Running Total, % of Total, YoY, Rank, etc.
  • Custom table calcs use functions like WINDOW_SUM, RUNNING_SUM, LOOKUP, RANK, INDEX
  • Δ triangle on a pill indicates a table calc is applied
  • Addressing fields: the dimension the calc moves along (direction)
  • Partitioning fields: dimensions that define separate groups (restart)
  • Edit Table Calculation: "Compute using" sets direction; Specific Dimensions for fine control
  • Common patterns: running totals, YoY %, moving averages, rank, percent of total
  • LOOKUP(expr, offset) accesses values at relative positions
  • FIRST(), LAST(), INDEX(), SIZE() give navigation within partition
  • RANK variants: RANK, RANK_DENSE, RANK_MODIFIED, RANK_UNIQUE, RANK_PERCENTILE
  • Table calc filters apply LAST in Order of Operations — useful for keeping rank stable
  • Table calcs depend on viz structure; LODs are viz-independent
  • Use table calcs for sequence-dependent metrics (running, growth, rank)
  • Use LODs for grain-shifting metrics (customer LTV, % of grand total)

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Parameters are user-driven inputs that change calculations, filter values, or what's displayed. They power the most interactive Tableau dashboards. The Specialist exam tests parameter creation, types, and using them in calculated fields and filters.

What parameters are

A parameter is a single named value the user can change

Examples:
 Sales target threshold (Number)
 Selected metric (List: "Sales", "Profit", "Orders")
 Top N value (Integer: 5, 10, 25, 50)
 Date range (Date or Date range)
 What-if scenarios (multiplier for forecasts)

Parameters are NOT data fields:
 They have no underlying data
 Single value at a time
 Used in calculated fields and filter conditions
 Shown to users via "Show Parameter" control

Distinction from filters:
 Filters narrow the data
 Parameters change WHAT or HOW calculations work

Creating a parameter

Right-click in Data pane → Create Parameter

Parameter dialog:
 Name: e.g., "Top N"
 Data type: Float / Integer / String / Boolean / Date / Date and time
 Current value: starting value
 Display format: how numeric/date values display
 
 Allowable values:
 All — user types any value
 List — drop-down or list of options
 Range — slider with min/max/step

Once created, parameter appears in Parameters section at bottom of Data pane
Right-click → Show Parameter → adds control to viz

Parameter types in detail

Number parameter (Top N)

Create "Top N" parameter:
 Data type: Integer
 Current value: 10
 Allowable values: Range
 Minimum: 1
 Maximum: 50
 Step: 1

Show parameter → slider appears
User adjusts → recalculation triggers

Use in filter:
 Filter on Customer Name → Top tab
 Top: [Parameters].[Top N] by SUM([Sales])
 Now "Top N customers" is user-controlled

List parameter (Selected Metric)

Create "Selected Metric" parameter:
 Data type: String
 Allowable values: List
 Add values:
 Display As Value
 "Sales" "Sales"
 "Profit" "Profit"
 "Orders" "Orders"

In a calculated field:
 Dynamic Measure =
 CASE [Selected Metric]
 WHEN "Sales" THEN SUM([Sales])
 WHEN "Profit" THEN SUM([Profit])
 WHEN "Orders" THEN COUNTD([Order ID])
 END

Drag Dynamic Measure to viz; show parameter
User changes selection → measure swaps

Date parameter (Reference Date)

Create "Reference Date" parameter:
 Data type: Date
 Current value: TODAY() or specific date
 Allowable values: All (or Range)

Use in calculations:
 Days From Reference = DATEDIFF('day', [Order Date], [Reference Date])

Or in filters:
 Show only orders within 30 days of reference date
 Filter [Order Date]: Range 
 Min: DATEADD('day', -30, [Reference Date])
 Max: [Reference Date]

Boolean parameter (Show Forecast)

Create "Show Forecast" parameter:
 Data type: Boolean
 Allowable values: All (True/False)

Use as a flag:
 Visible Series =
 IF [Show Forecast] OR [Year] <= 2024 THEN SUM([Sales])
 ELSE NULL
 END

Or with Sets / dynamic visibility:
 Several patterns leverage boolean parameters for toggle behaviors

Showing the parameter control

Right-click parameter → Show Parameter
 Parameter control appears in right side panel

Control type (right-click control → choose):
 Slider — number with range
 Compact slider — smaller slider
 Type In — text input
 Type In and Slider — both
 Single value list — radio buttons
 Multiple value list — checkboxes (NEW; was single only for years)
 Dropdown — compact dropdown

Customize:
 Display title
 Number format
 Layout style
 Fit (size)

Parameter actions (dynamic parameter changes)

Introduced in 2019.2: parameters can update from user clicks on viz

Setup:
 Worksheet menu → Actions → Add Action → Change Parameter

Configuration:
 Source sheet (where user clicks)
 Target parameter (which to update)
 Field used to set value (which field's value passes to parameter)
 Run on: Hover / Select / Menu

Example:
 Bar chart of regions
 Click a region → Region Parameter updates → other vizzes filter accordingly

Use cases:
 - Drill-down navigation (click bar → set parameter → other views update)
 - "What-if" pickers
 - Replace static slicers with click-driven selection

Workbook-wide parameter usage

Parameters are workbook-level (not per-sheet)
 - Same parameter value across all sheets in the workbook
 - One parameter, many calc fields and filters reference it
 - Change once → all dependent vizzes update

Best practices:
 - Name parameters clearly: "p_TopN" or "Top N (parameter)"
 - Group all parameters at top of Data pane
 - Use comments in calc fields explaining which parameter drives what
 - Show parameters near the vizzes they affect (or at top of dashboard)

Dynamic axis with parameters

Pattern: let user choose what's on x-axis

Create "X Axis" parameter:
 List: ["Region", "Category", "Sub-Category", "Customer Segment"]

Calculated dimension:
 Dynamic Dim =
 CASE [X Axis]
 WHEN "Region" THEN [Region]
 WHEN "Category" THEN [Category]
 WHEN "Sub-Category" THEN [Sub-Category]
 WHEN "Customer Segment" THEN [Customer Segment]
 END

Drag Dynamic Dim to Columns
Show "X Axis" parameter
User picks → entire viz reorganizes

Caveat: all options must be similar type (here all strings)
For mixing types, build separate sheets and use bookmarks/swaps

Reference line via parameter

Add a user-controlled threshold line:

1. Create "Target" parameter (Float, e.g., 50000)
2. Right-click axis → Add Reference Line
3. Value: select [Target] parameter
4. Format the line (color, label)

User changes Target → line moves in real time

Combine with conditional formatting:
 Color =
 IF [SUM(Sales)] >= [Target] THEN "Above Target"
 ELSE "Below Target"
 END

Use this Color field on Marks card → green/red bars based on user-set threshold

Parameters in titles and labels

Reference parameters in titles for dynamic context:

Edit sheet title:
 Click title bar → Edit Title
 Insert parameter via menu or type:
 Sales for Top  Customers
 
 At runtime, the title becomes:
 Sales for Top 10 Customers

Same in:
 - Tooltip text
 - Annotation text
 - Reference line labels
 - Caption (bottom of worksheet)

This makes dashboards feel responsive to user choices

Worked example — interactive sales explorer

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Parameter-driven dashboard
// Goal: dashboard where user controls multiple aspects via parameters

// Parameter 1: Metric Selector
// String list: "Sales", "Profit", "Orders", "Customers"
Selected Metric param

// Parameter 2: Top N
// Integer range 5-50, step 5
Top N param

// Parameter 3: Date Range Months
// Integer range 1-24
Date Range Months param

// Parameter 4: Show Target
// Boolean
Show Target param

// Parameter 5: Target Value
// Float, default 100000
Target Value param

// Calculated Dynamic Measure
Dynamic Metric =
 CASE [Selected Metric]
 WHEN "Sales" THEN SUM([Sales])
 WHEN "Profit" THEN SUM([Profit])
 WHEN "Orders" THEN COUNTD([Order ID])
 WHEN "Customers" THEN COUNTD([Customer ID])
 END

// Filter: Top N by [Dynamic Metric]
// Add Customer Name filter → Top tab → 
// Top [Top N] by [Dynamic Metric]

// Filter: Date Range
// Add [Order Date] filter →
// Range: DATEADD('month', -[Date Range Months], TODAY()) to TODAY()

// Reference line:
// Add reference line at [Target Value]
// Only shown if [Show Target] = TRUE

// Dynamic title:

// (last  months)"

// Show all parameters on dashboard

// One sheet handles 4 different "views"

Common parameter mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Forgetting to Show Parameter — user has no way to change it
  2. Wrong data type — number parameter used as string fails comparisons
  3. Trying multi-select on parameter — parameters are single-value
  4. Confusing parameter with filter — different purposes
  5. Hardcoded values in calc instead of parameter — defeats the purpose
  6. Mixing types in dynamic dim/measure — keep all options same type
  7. Forgetting to use parameter in calc — calc not driven by parameter
  8. Out-of-range parameter values from old workbooks
  9. Parameter title not updating — needs explicit Edit Title with insertion
  10. Parameter action not connected — Worksheet → Actions setup required
★ ON THE EXAM

"User-driven single value?" → Parameter.

"Create parameter?" → Right-click in Data pane → Create Parameter.

"Show parameter?" → Right-click parameter → Show Parameter.

"Parameter data types?" → Float, Integer, String, Boolean, Date, DateTime.

"Allowable values?" → All / List / Range.

"Top N controlled by user?" → Number parameter + Top filter using parameter.

"Swap measure?" → String list parameter + CASE in calc field.

"Dynamic axis?" → Parameter + CASE in calc dimension.

"Reference line at user-set value?" → Right-click axis → Add Reference Line → use parameter.

"Insert parameter in title?" → Edit title → Insert → Parameter.

"Parameter changes via click?" → Parameter Action (Worksheet → Actions).

"Parameter scope?" → Workbook-wide (not per-sheet).

"Parameter vs filter?" → Parameter changes calc/value; filter narrows data.

"Multiple values?" → Not with parameters; use sets or filters.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Parameters are single named values users can change to drive calculations and filters
  • Parameters are workbook-wide; affect any calc/filter that references them
  • Create via right-click in Data pane → Create Parameter
  • Data types: Float, Integer, String, Boolean, Date, DateTime
  • Allowable values: All (free input), List (dropdown options), Range (slider)
  • Show Parameter to expose as interactive control on viz
  • Common parameter use: Top N (Integer), Selected Metric (String list), threshold (Float), date
  • Use CASE in calculated field to swap measures or dimensions based on parameter
  • Reference lines can use parameter values for user-controlled thresholds
  • Insert parameters in titles, tooltips, captions, and reference line labels for dynamic display
  • Parameter Actions (2019.2+): clicks on viz update parameter dynamically
  • Parameters are SINGLE-VALUE only; for multi-select use sets or filters
  • Parameters do NOT narrow data; filters do
  • Combine parameters with filters and calcs for fully interactive dashboards
  • Workbook-level scope: one parameter, many dependent vizzes update together

A workbook usually has multiple sheets, but users see DASHBOARDS — combined views of related charts with interactivity. Layout choices determine usability. The Specialist exam tests dashboard sizing, layout containers, and adding objects.

Creating a dashboard

Click the New Dashboard tab at bottom of workbook
 (icon: grid with squares)

The dashboard editor opens:
 Left side: Dashboard pane
 - Size settings
 - Sheets list (drag onto canvas)
 - Objects list (drag elements like text, image, container)
 Center: dashboard canvas
 
 Layout pane (toggle via tab at top of left panel):
 - Hierarchical tree of objects
 - Position, size, padding

Add sheets:
 Drag from Sheets list onto canvas
 Sheet appears at chosen position
 Drop zones (highlighted) show where it'll snap

Dashboard size

Set in left panel under Size

Options:
 Fixed size:
 Specify exact pixel dimensions (e.g., 1280 × 800)
 Same regardless of browser size
 Use when controlling exact layout
 Common presets: Desktop, Tablet, Phone

 Range:
 Min/max dimensions
 Resizes within range

 Automatic:
 Adapts to browser size
 Risky: layouts can break at unusual sizes

Common standard sizes:
 Desktop browser: 1366 × 768 (laptop) or 1920 × 1080 (HD)
 Default desktop: 1000 × 800
 iPad landscape: 1024 × 768
 iPad portrait: 768 × 1024
 Mobile: 375 × 667 (iPhone-ish)

Best practice:
 Start with Fixed; design carefully
 Add Phone layout separately for mobile (covered later)

Tiled vs Floating

TiledFloating
Snaps to grid; uses containersFree positioning; overlaps allowed
Auto-resizes with siblingsStays at set position
Default; predictable layoutFor decoration, logos, badges
Resizes with dashboardDoesn't resize automatically

To toggle: select object → on Layout pane, choose Tiled or Floating.

Layout containers

Layout containers are invisible boxes that group sheets/objects together

Two types:
 Horizontal: places contents left-to-right
 Vertical: places contents top-to-bottom

Adding:
 Drag Horizontal or Vertical from Objects panel onto canvas

Inside a container:
 Drag sheets into it
 They auto-arrange in container's direction
 Resize within container via blue lines

Why use containers:
 - Clean alignment
 - Group related sheets logically
 - Easy resizing (drag container handle to resize children proportionally)
 - Add titles/headers per section

Nested containers:
 Horizontal inside Vertical (rows of columns)
 Common for complex layouts

Objects panel

Drag from Objects section in dashboard pane:

Horizontal — layout container (auto left-to-right)
Vertical — layout container (auto top-to-bottom)
Text — add text box (heading, description, instructions)
Image — add image / logo
Web Page — embed a webpage URL (web object)
Blank — empty space (transparent gap)
Navigation — button for inter-dashboard navigation
Download — button to download as PDF/PowerPoint/Image/Crosstab
Extension — Tableau Extensions (third-party add-ons)
Ask Data — search bar (Q&A-style natural language)
Show Toggle — show/hide layout containers
Filter — exposed filter widget

Resizing and positioning

Tiled objects:
 Hover edge between two siblings → drag blue line
 Resizes both proportionally
 Limited to within parent container

Floating objects:
 Drag corner handles
 Drag the whole object to move
 Position: pixel-level via Layout pane

Layout pane:
 Shows tree of all objects
 Properties: position (x, y), size (w, h)
 Padding: inner space around content
 Background: color or transparency
 Border: line around object

Pro tip:
 Use Layout pane to set EXACT sizes
 Drag fine-tuning is approximate

Common dashboard layouts

Header + content

Vertical container (outer)
 Text object: "Sales Dashboard" (banner)
 Horizontal container (KPI row)
 KPI 1 (sheet)
 KPI 2 (sheet)
 KPI 3 (sheet)
 Horizontal container (main row)
 Vertical container (left column)
 Chart 1
 Chart 2
 Big chart (right)
 
 Footer: Text "Updated "

Side filter panel

Horizontal container (outer)
 Vertical container (left, 200px wide)
 Title
 Filter 1 widget
 Filter 2 widget
 Filter 3 widget
 Vertical container (right, fill width)
 Header
 Charts in grid

Dashboard with tabs

Use Show/Hide toggle:
 Stack multiple containers at the same position
 Use buttons or parameter to drive visibility
 Show only one at a time

Or use multiple dashboards:
 Dashboard tabs at bottom (separate dashboards)
 Use navigation buttons between them

Show / Hide containers

Drag Show / Hide button from Objects → onto a layout container

Configure:
 Right-click the toggle button → Item shown text, Item hidden text
 Choose icon or text
 Click button → toggles container's visibility

Use cases:
 - Collapsible filter panel (hide when not needed)
 - Toggle between charts on same canvas
 - Reveal details on demand

Limitations:
 Works on entire CONTAINER (not individual sheets)
 Container must be visible to start, or you can't see the toggle

Dashboard text and images

Text objects:
 Drag Text from Objects panel
 Double-click → edit content
 Rich formatting: font, size, color, alignment
 Reference parameters/fields:
 Insert → Sheets → Field/Parameter

Image objects:
 Drag Image → choose file
 Resize via handles
 Set background transparency, fit (Center / Fit Image / Fit Tile)
 Add URL for hyperlink behavior (click → opens browser)

Web page object:
 Drag Web Page → enter URL
 Embedded iframe-like
 Common: embed YouTube tutorial, external doc, monitoring tool
 URL Action can change the URL dynamically based on clicked mark

Dashboard title

Dashboard menu → Show Title (toggle)

Title displays the dashboard name (or custom text)
Edit:
 Double-click title bar
 Add parameters / dynamic text

Format:
 Right-click title → Format Title
 Font, color, size, alignment

Worked example — sales overview dashboard

Best practices for dashboards

★ DESIGN GUIDELINES
  • Limit to ~6-8 charts per dashboard — more becomes overwhelming
  • Most important info at top-left — natural reading flow
  • Consistent spacing and alignment via containers
  • Use white space — don't fill every pixel
  • Title and subtitle set context immediately
  • Filters near the data they affect
  • Color consistency — same color = same meaning across charts
  • Match audience — executives want overview; analysts want detail
  • Mobile view separately configured if needed
  • Test on actual device — desktop preview doesn't show mobile reality

Common dashboard mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Automatic size + complex layout — breaks at unexpected sizes
  2. Free-floating everything — hard to maintain; use containers
  3. Too many charts — 15+ visuals overwhelm
  4. Forgetting fit settings on individual sheets (Standard vs Entire View)
  5. Misaligned headers/subtitles — use containers for consistency
  6. Filters not connected to multiple sheets — change "Apply to Worksheets"
  7. No mobile layout when needed — phone view is configured separately
  8. Show/Hide toggle nesting confusion — keep one toggle per container
  9. Dashboard "fits" but charts truncate — adjust individual sheet fits
  10. Web Page object embedding external sites that don't allow embedding — X-Frame-Options
★ ON THE EXAM

"Create dashboard?" → New Dashboard tab at bottom.

"Dashboard size?" → Left panel → Size → Fixed / Range / Automatic.

"Add sheet?" → Drag from Sheets list to canvas.

"Tiled vs Floating?" → Tiled snaps to grid; Floating is free-positioned.

"Layout containers?" → Horizontal (left-to-right) or Vertical (top-to-bottom).

"Common objects?" → Text, Image, Web Page, Blank, Navigation, Download, Extension.

"Show/Hide button?" → Drag from Objects to layout container; toggles visibility.

"Embed webpage?" → Web Page object with URL.

"Dynamic title?" → Edit title → Insert parameter or field.

"Side-by-side layout?" → Horizontal container.

"Stacked vertical layout?" → Vertical container.

"Resize between sheets?" → Drag the blue line between them.

"Phone layout?" → Configured separately under Device Designer.

"Best practice number of charts?" → 6-8 max per dashboard.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Create a dashboard via the New Dashboard tab; drag sheets from the Dashboard pane
  • Size options: Fixed (pixels), Range (min/max), Automatic — Fixed gives most predictable layout
  • Tiled objects snap to a grid; Floating objects can be placed anywhere and overlap
  • Layout containers (Horizontal / Vertical) group and auto-arrange contents
  • Drag containers from Objects panel; nest them for complex layouts
  • Objects available: Text, Image, Web Page, Blank, Navigation, Download, Extension, Ask Data
  • Show / Hide toggle: button hides/shows entire layout container
  • Dashboard title: Dashboard menu → Show Title; editable with parameters and fields
  • Text objects can include parameter / field references for dynamic content
  • Image objects accept files; can have URL hyperlink action
  • Web Page object embeds external URLs (iframe-style)
  • Limit dashboards to 6-8 charts for clarity
  • Use containers for clean alignment; avoid free-floating everywhere
  • Phone layouts configured separately under Device Designer
  • Test layout at intended viewing size — Range/Automatic can break unexpectedly
