◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Dashboard actions transform a static collection of charts into an interactive analytical tool. Click a bar, filter another chart. Hover a point, highlight related data. Click a customer, jump to detail. The Specialist exam tests action types and configuration.

Action types overview

ActionWhat it does
FilterClicking marks filters other sheets
HighlightClicking marks highlights related ones
URL (Go to URL)Opens a webpage based on clicked data
Go to SheetNavigate to another sheet/dashboard
Change ParameterClick updates a parameter value
Change SetClick adds/removes from a set

Setting up actions

Dashboard menu → Actions → Add Action

Or on a worksheet:
 Worksheet menu → Actions → Add Action

Action dialog:
 Name — descriptive (e.g., "Filter sales by region click")
 Run on action:
 Hover — fires when hovering
 Select — fires on click
 Menu — appears in right-click menu
 Source Sheets — which sheets trigger the action
 Target Sheets — which sheets respond
 Other options — specific to action type
 Clearing the selection — what happens when user deselects

Filter actions

Filter action: clicking marks in source → filters target sheets

Configuration:
 Source: sheets where user clicks
 Target: sheets to filter
 Run on: Select (most common)
 
 Target Filters:
 All Fields — pass all dimensions from clicked mark
 Selected Fields — choose which dims pass

 Clearing the selection:
 Leave the filter — filter stays when user deselects
 Show all values — return to unfiltered (recommended)
 Exclude all values — empty viz when nothing selected

Quick filter action:
 Dashboard → Click on a sheet → Use as filter (funnel icon at top of sheet)
 Automatic setup with sensible defaults

Use cases:
 Click bar in region chart → other charts filter to that region
 Click customer in table → details panel shows that customer

Highlight actions

Highlight action: clicking marks dims unrelated; highlights matching ones

Differs from filter:
 Filter: hides non-matching rows
 Highlight: shows all rows but visually emphasizes matching

Configuration:
 Source / Target sheets
 Field(s) to match on (e.g., Region)
 Run on: Hover (common for highlight) or Select

Visual effect:
 Marks not matching: faded
 Marks matching: full color

Use cases:
 Click region → bars in other chart darken to show same region
 Hover customer → related orders highlight

URL actions

URL action: clicking opens a URL (browser or Web Page object)

Configuration:
 URL template:
 Hardcoded: https://example.com/dashboard
 Dynamic: https://crm.example.com/customer/
 → "" inserts the clicked mark's field value

Open in:
 New tab — fresh browser tab
 Current tab — replaces page
 Web Page object — within dashboard (Web Page must already exist)

Use cases:
 Click customer → opens CRM customer page
 Click product → opens product spec page
 Click region → opens regional intranet

Go to Sheet action (navigation)

Filter action with "Go to Sheet" option:
 Source sheet → target sheet (different sheet or dashboard)
 Clicked field values filter the destination
 Like drillthrough in Power BI

Configuration:
 Source: where user clicks
 Target: sheet to navigate to
 Run on: Menu (right-click) or Select
 Target filter: which field to pass

Best practice:
 Add Navigation button on destination → "Back" button
 Use Run on: Menu so users don't accidentally navigate

Use cases:
 Click customer → jump to customer detail page filtered to that customer
 Click product → jump to product analytics

Change Parameter action

Click on a mark → updates a parameter value (introduced 2019.2)

Configuration:
 Source sheets / fields
 Target parameter: which parameter to update
 Source field: which clicked field's value passes to parameter
 Aggregation: how multi-value selection handled
 Clearing the selection: what value to set if nothing selected

Use case:
 Bar chart of regions
 Click "East" → Region Parameter = "East"
 Other dashboards / calcs use this parameter
 Replaces typical filter widget with click-to-select

Best practice:
 Parameter actions feel native; users don't need to know filters
 Combine with parameter-driven measures or filters
 Show parameter on dashboard so current value is visible

Change Set action

Click on a mark → adds/removes members from a set

Configuration:
 Source field: which dim values are added to set
 Target set: which set to modify
 Run on: Select / Hover / Menu
 Selection behavior:
 Assign values to set — replace current set members
 Add values to set — append to existing
 Remove values from set — opposite

Use case:
 Set "Selected Customers" starts empty
 User clicks customers → set updates dynamically
 Other vizzes can use set for color highlighting or filtering

Set actions enable "Drill into selection" workflows
Same set can be used in many calc fields and filters across the dashboard

Multiple actions on one source

A single sheet can be the source of MULTIPLE actions

Example:
 Action 1: Filter regional chart by region (Run on: Select)
 Action 2: Change parameter "Selected Region" (Run on: Select)
 Action 3: Highlight related orders in another chart (Run on: Hover)
 Action 4: Right-click → drillthrough to customer detail (Run on: Menu)

All fire simultaneously based on event type
Test thoroughly — some combinations conflict

Action menu

When an action's "Run on" is set to Menu:
 Right-click a mark in source viz
 See action label in context menu
 Click to fire

Useful for:
 - Drill-through to other dashboards (don't want hover firing)
 - URL actions (deliberate navigation)
 - Avoiding accidental clicks

Configure menu label:
 Action dialog has "Name" field — appears in context menu

Multiple menu actions:
 All show as items in the right-click menu
 User picks which to fire

Worked example — interactive sales dashboard

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — 4-action dashboard
// Dashboard layout:
// Top: Map of regions (sales)
// Mid: Bar chart of top customers
// Bot: Detail table

// Action 1: Filter action
// Source: Map
// Target: Bar chart, Detail table
// Field: Region
// Run on: Select
// Clearing: Show all values
// Behavior: Click region on map → other vizzes filter to it

// Action 2: Highlight action
// Source: Bar chart
// Target: Map
// Field: Region
// Run on: Hover
// Behavior: Hover customer → their region highlights on map

// Action 3: URL action
// Source: Detail table
// URL: https://crm.example.com/customer/
// Run on: Menu
// Open in: New tab
// Behavior: Right-click customer → CRM in new tab

// Action 4: Parameter action
// Source: Map
// Target parameter: Selected Region
// Field: Region
// Run on: Select
// Behavior: Click region → parameter updates → title/calcs respond

// User flow:
// Click California on map → bar chart and table filter to California
// Hover bar in customer chart → California highlights again
// Right-click customer → opens CRM
// Title says "Sales for California" (parameter-driven)

Dashboard URL targeting Web Page object

If your dashboard has a Web Page object:
 URL Action can target the Web Page object instead of new browser tab

Setup:
 Place Web Page object on dashboard
 URL Action → "URL Target" → Web Page object name
 Now clicking marks updates the embedded webpage

Example:
 Embedded map showing route
 Click order → embedded webpage shows delivery tracking
 Click product → embedded webpage shows spec sheet

This keeps users in the dashboard rather than navigating away

Common dashboard action mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Click-to-filter on every chart — overwhelming; pick deliberately
  2. Action target same as source — clicking self-filters; usually unintended
  3. "Leave the filter" when "Show all" is desired — viz gets stuck filtered
  4. Hover actions on slow charts — performance issues
  5. URL with hardcoded value instead of reference
  6. Set action without using the set — change has no effect
  7. Multiple conflicting actions firing same event
  8. Parameter action without parameter shown — user doesn't see current value
  9. Forgetting "Run on Menu" for drillthrough — accidental clicks navigate away
  10. External URL embeds blocked — X-Frame-Options header denies it
★ ON THE EXAM

"Action types?" → Filter, Highlight, URL, Go to Sheet, Change Parameter, Change Set.

"Where set up?" → Dashboard menu → Actions → Add Action.

"Click filters other sheets?" → Filter action.

"Click visually emphasizes related?" → Highlight action.

"Click opens URL?" → URL action with template.

"Insert field in URL template?" → syntax.

"Click sets parameter?" → Parameter action (2019.2+).

"Click changes set membership?" → Set action.

"Right-click only?" → Run on: Menu.

"Hover triggers?" → Run on: Hover.

"After deselect?" → Clearing the selection: Show all / Leave / Exclude.

"Click sheet, use as filter?" → Click sheet on dashboard → funnel icon at top.

"Navigate to another sheet filtered?" → Go to Sheet (a type of filter action with target sheet).

"Update Web Page object?" → URL action with URL Target = Web Page object.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Dashboard actions make dashboards interactive: clicks/hovers trigger behavior
  • Six action types: Filter, Highlight, URL, Go to Sheet, Change Parameter, Change Set
  • Filter action: clicking marks filters target sheets
  • Highlight action: clicking marks emphasizes related marks (no filtering)
  • URL action: opens URL with dynamic field substitution via
  • Go to Sheet: navigate to another sheet/dashboard, filtered by clicked field
  • Change Parameter (2019.2+): clicks update a parameter value
  • Change Set: clicks add/remove members from a set dynamically
  • Configure via Dashboard menu → Actions → Add Action
  • Run on: Hover (immediate), Select (click), or Menu (right-click)
  • Clearing the selection: Leave filter, Show all (recommended), Exclude all
  • Quick filter: click sheet → funnel icon at top → uses sheet as filter
  • Multiple actions can fire from the same source on different events
  • Use Menu run-on for drillthrough to prevent accidental navigation
  • URL actions can target Web Page objects on the dashboard, keeping users in context

Tableau Public reality: it is free — and every workbook you publish is PUBLICLY accessible to anyone; never publish private data there.

Gridlines come off through Format › Worksheet › Borders and Lines › Grid Lines › None. The row lines, column lines and zero line are three separate settings — clearing gridlines does not remove the zero line, which is usually the one you want to keep as the reference baseline.

Stories let you string together views to tell a narrative — think slideshow with insights. They're useful for presentations, executive summaries, and walkthrough analyses. The Specialist exam tests creating stories, navigator captions, and story points.

What stories are

A Story is a SEQUENCE of dashboards and sheets with a narrative caption per step
 - Each step is called a "Story Point"
 - Users navigate forward/backward through points
 - Each point can have a title (caption) explaining the insight

Distinction from dashboard:
 Dashboard = single view combining multiple sheets
 Story = sequence of dashboards/sheets, navigable

Use cases:
 - Walking through an analysis: "Here's the problem... here's the cause... here's the fix"
 - Executive summary with key insights ordered
 - Onboarding new users to a dataset
 - Storytelling-style data journalism

Creating a story

Click the New Story tab at bottom of workbook (storyboard icon)

Story editor:
 Left side: Story pane
 - Story size settings
 - Dashboards / sheets list (drag into story)
 - Story Description (optional intro text)
 Center: story canvas with caption bar at top
 Bottom: story points navigator

Add story points:
 Drag a dashboard or sheet from list onto canvas
 Or click "Blank" → empty story point
 Each addition creates a new point in the navigator at top

Story size and layout

Stories have their own size (separate from dashboards):
 Story size settings on left
 Common: 1024 × 768, 1366 × 768

Story layout:
 Caption bar at top (story navigation strip)
 Story content area (where dashboards/sheets render)

Caption position:
 Story menu → Show Story Title (default on)
 Each story point has a navigator button

Caption styles:
 Caption Boxes — text in colored boxes at top (default)
 Numbers — just 1, 2, 3 buttons
 Dots — small dots (compact)
 Arrows only — minimal navigation

Story points

Each story point is one slide in the narrative

Add point:
 Drag dashboard/sheet to canvas
 Or "Blank" → manually build content
 Or "Duplicate" current point and modify

Edit point caption:
 Click on caption box → type description
 Examples:
 "Q4 sales declined 12% YoY"
 "The drop was concentrated in Region X"
 "Root cause: supply chain disruption"

Point order:
 Drag captions in the navigator to reorder
 Right-click → Delete to remove

Each point captures:
 - Current sheet/dashboard view
 - Filter/parameter values at the moment of save
 - Visible visual selections (highlights)
 - Caption text

Story navigation options

Story menu → Format → Navigator Style:
 Caption boxes — colored boxes, default
 Numbers — numbered list
 Dots — compact dots
 Arrows only — minimal

Show Navigator: toggle on/off

Visible navigation buttons:
 Show update button — appears when story point needs updating
 Show navigator — yes/no
 Show description — yes/no

Story interactions:
 Users click captions in navigator to jump to points
 Left/Right arrows scroll through points
 Each point is a "snapshot" of the underlying view

Updating story points

If you modify the underlying dashboard AFTER creating a story point:
 Story point shows an "update needed" indicator
 Two choices:
 Update: refreshes point with new dashboard state
 Save as new: creates additional point with new state

Common workflow:
 Build dashboard → add as story point
 Modify dashboard (change filters, add visuals)
 Add another story point showing the new state
 Stack of points becomes the narrative arc

Avoid:
 Updating live → lose previous version
 Always save as new if uncertain

Caption formatting

Click caption text box to edit
Format options:
 Font, size, color
 Background color
 Border / shadow

Best practice for captions:
 - Keep short: 5-15 words
 - Lead with the INSIGHT, not the data
 - "Sales fell 12% in Q4" (good)
 - "Q4 sales chart" (bad — describes, doesn't tell story)

Use consistent caption style across all points
Set the visual tone for your audience

Story description

Optional intro/conclusion text:
 Left panel → drag Description into the story
 Edit text inline

Use for:
 - "Introduction: This analysis covers Q4 2024 performance"
 - "Methodology" or "Data sources" footer
 - "Recommendations" closing point

Description blocks appear at the position you drop them
Common: intro at top, conclusion at end

Worked example — sales analysis story

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — 6-point sales narrative
// Story title: "Q4 2024 Sales Performance Review"

// Point 1 (Description / Intro)
// "Executive summary of Q4 2024 sales performance"
// "Key metrics, regional breakdown, and recommended actions"

// Point 2 (Dashboard: Overall KPIs)
// Caption: "Q4 sales hit $4.2M — down 8% YoY"
// Snapshot: KPI cards showing totals + YoY %

// Point 3 (Dashboard: Regional Breakdown filtered to top regions)
// Caption: "Decline concentrated in North America (-15%)"
// Snapshot: regional bar chart with NA highlighted
// Filter: Region = North America

// Point 4 (Dashboard: Product Detail)
// Caption: "Hardware sales dropped 22% due to supply chain"
// Snapshot: product chart filtered to NA hardware

// Point 5 (Dashboard: Forecast / Recovery Plan)
// Caption: "Recovery plan: software push expected to offset"
// Snapshot: forecast view with parameter-set targets

// Point 6 (Description / Conclusion)
// "Recommended Actions:
// 1. Diversify hardware suppliers
// 2. Increase software marketing budget
// 3. Monitor weekly through Q1 2025"

// Result: a 6-step narrative that walks readers from
// problem → cause → context → recommendation

Story vs dashboard — when to use which

StoryDashboard
Sequential narrativeFree exploration
Linear walkthroughUser chooses what to focus on
For presentations / reportsFor interactive analysis
Captions tell key insightsUser reads charts themselves
Best for executive summariesBest for daily operational use

Common story mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Too many story points — keep to 5-8 for readability
  2. Captions describe instead of tell story — lead with insight
  3. Forgetting to save view state — filters change before saving
  4. Inconsistent caption style across points
  5. Updating points instead of duplicating — lose narrative version
  6. Stories without intro/conclusion — feels like a slideshow without context
  7. Mixing dashboards and sheets sloppily — keep style consistent
  8. Stories as a substitute for proper dashboards — different tools
  9. Forgetting that filters in story points are snapshots — user can't drill freely
  10. Long story descriptions instead of multiple points — break content into steps
★ ON THE EXAM

"Create story?" → New Story tab at bottom of workbook.

"Sequential narrative?" → Story (vs dashboard for exploration).

"Each step in a story?" → Story Point.

"Caption on each point?" → Text describing the insight.

"Add a point?" → Drag dashboard/sheet onto canvas.

"Reorder points?" → Drag captions in navigator at top.

"Empty point?" → Drag "Blank" from left panel.

"Text-only step?" → Drag "Description" from left panel.

"Update vs save as new?" → Save as new preserves the previous point.

"Navigator styles?" → Caption boxes, Numbers, Dots, Arrows only.

"Recommended points per story?" → 5-8 for clarity.

"Stories vs dashboards?" → Stories = linear narrative; Dashboards = free exploration.

"Caption best practice?" → State the insight, not just describe the chart.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Stories are sequential collections of dashboards/sheets with narrative captions
  • Each step is called a Story Point; users navigate forward/backward
  • Create via New Story tab at the bottom of the workbook
  • Drag dashboards/sheets into the story to create points; each captures the current view
  • Each point has a caption — keep short and lead with the insight
  • Add Description objects for text-only intro/conclusion steps
  • Reorder points by dragging captions in the navigator
  • Update story points when underlying dashboard changes (with care; or save as new)
  • Navigator styles: caption boxes (default), numbers, dots, arrows only
  • Limit to 5-8 points for clarity
  • Stories are ideal for executive presentations and walkthroughs
  • Dashboards are better for interactive exploration
  • Captions are key — they convey the analytical insight
  • Each point snapshots the view + filters + parameters at save time
  • Use story description for intro / conclusion / methodology context

Server facts: the permission ladder from lowest to highest — Viewer, Explorer, Creator, Site Admin. Embedding a view in a web page uses the EMBED CODE — an iframe snippet or the Tableau JavaScript API.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The Tableau Desktop Specialist exam has predictable traps and well-known gotcha questions. Recognizing them in advance saves time and avoids point losses on test day.

Trap 1: Dimension vs measure confusion

Question pattern:
 "ZIP code is auto-classified as a measure. What should you do?"

Trap:
 Tempted to "leave it as is" or use it as-is in viz

Correct:
 Convert to dimension (right-click → Convert to Dimension)
 ZIP codes shouldn't be SUMmed
 Same for: Customer ID, Year (numeric), any identifier-like number

Why exam tests this:
 Tableau auto-detects numeric → measure
 But numeric identifiers are categorical in nature
 Common practical issue

Trap 2: Date Part vs Date Value

Question pattern:
 "You want a line chart showing sales month by month over multiple years.
 Months should be on a continuous timeline."

Trap:
 Selecting MONTH as discrete (blue): each month name groups across years
 Selecting MONTH as Date Part: same problem

Correct:
 MONTH as continuous Date VALUE (green pill)
 Each month-year becomes a separate point on continuous time axis

Memorize:
 Date Part = name/number (e.g., "January", 1)
 Date Value = actual date (e.g., 2024-01-01)
 Discrete = blue = headers
 Continuous = green = axis

For "trend over time": want continuous Date Value
For "compare months across years": want discrete Date Part

Trap 3: Group vs Set

Question pattern:
 "You want to flag top 10 customers dynamically so the viz updates as data changes."

Trap:
 Create a Group of those customers (becomes static)

Correct:
 Create a SET with Top N condition by sales
 Group = fixed manual combine values
 Set = dynamic IN/OUT marking (often Top N or Condition-based)

Other variations:
 "Combine NYC, NY, N.Y.C. into one value" → Group
 "Mark customers with > 10 orders" → Set (Condition-based)
 "Highlight top 5 products by sales" → Set (Top tab)

Trap 4: Order of Operations

Question pattern:
 "You apply a Top 10 filter and a Region filter. You select region 'East'.
 Why does the viz show only 3 customers instead of the expected 10?"

Trap:
 Assuming Top 10 applies to East subset

Correct:
 Top N filter applies BEFORE dimension filter (Region)
 So Top 10 = top 10 customers GLOBALLY
 Then Region filter narrows to East
 Only the few global top 10 that bought in East show

Fix:
 Add Region filter to Context (right-click → Add to Context)
 Now Region becomes a context filter
 Top 10 runs AFTER context → top 10 within East

Memorize the order:
 Extract → Data Source → Context → FIXED → Dimension → INCLUDE/EXCLUDE → Measure → Table Calc

Trap 5: FIXED vs INCLUDE/EXCLUDE

Question pattern:
 "Each order should show that customer's total lifetime spend in a column."

Trap:
 Using INCLUDE — wrong; INCLUDE adds dim to viz grain
 Using SUM(Sales) — gives current row's amount, not customer total

Correct:
 {FIXED [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])}
 Same value repeats per customer's orders
 Customer total ignores viz's order-level grain

INCLUDE use case:
 "Average sales per customer in each region" 
 → AVG({INCLUDE [Customer] : SUM([Sales])})
 Need INCLUDE because Customer isn't in viz (Region is)
 
EXCLUDE use case:
 "Show each product's % of category total"
 → SUM(Sales) / {EXCLUDE [Product] : SUM(Sales)}
 When viz has both Product and Category, EXCLUDE Product gives category total

Trap 6: Live vs Extract performance

Question pattern:
 "Your dashboard is slow on a large transactional database. What should you do?"

Trap:
 "Optimize SQL" (not in scope for exam)

Correct:
 Switch from Live to Extract
 Extract creates compressed .hyper file
 Queries run against extract; much faster
 Refresh extract on a schedule

Or:
 Add Data Source filters to limit rows in extract
 Pre-aggregate during extract creation
 Use Incremental refresh for large fact tables

Question variant:
 "You need real-time data and database is fast." → Live
 "Performance matters, data can be a day old." → Extract

Trap 7: Joins vs Relationships

Question pattern:
 "Sales table joined with Order Items table inflates totals because each order
 has multiple items. How to fix?"

Trap:
 Use COUNTD or write complex LOD to deduplicate

Correct (modern way):
 Use Relationships instead of Joins
 Tableau queries each table at correct granularity
 No fan-out, no duplication

Old way (still in some questions):
 Joins force a single physical table; duplicates happen
 LOD expressions or careful aggregation needed to handle

Recognize:
 Relationships introduced 2020.2; default now
 Drag tables to canvas without entering physical layer = Relationship
 Double-click table to enter physical layer = Joins

Trap 8: Data blending limitations

Question pattern:
 "Your blend isn't working. The secondary source isn't filtering properly."

Common causes:
 Orange chain icon not active on the link field
 Field names don't auto-match (need Edit Blend Relationships)
 Trying to drill below primary's grain (impossible with blends)

Question variant:
 "Should you use blend, cross-database join, or relationship?"

Quick decision:
 Same source, similar grain → Relationships
 Different sources, similar grain → Cross-database join
 Different sources, different grain → Blending
 Per-sheet flexibility → Blending

Trap 9: Filter shelf vs Marks card

Question pattern:
 "Drag a field to Color on Marks card and expect it to filter data."

Trap:
 Confusing visual encoding with filtering

Correct:
 Filters shelf: restricts WHICH ROWS appear
 Marks card slots (Color, Size, etc.): encode existing rows visually
 
 Drag dimension to Color → all values shown, each gets a different color
 Drag dimension to Filters → only selected values remain

Trap 10: Synchronize Axis

Question pattern:
 "Your dual-axis chart shows misleading proportions. How to fix?"

Trap:
 Assuming default dual-axis sync's the scales

Correct:
 Right-click second axis → Synchronize Axis
 Default: each axis has its own scale (can mislead)
 Synchronized: both axes use same scale (when comparing magnitudes)

Question variant:
 "When NOT to synchronize?" 
 → When two measures have very different scales (e.g., Sales in $M and orders in count)
 → Keep separate axes to make both readable
 → Make sure labels are crystal clear

Always think: do these scales NEED to be comparable?

Trap 11: Drill down on hierarchies

Question pattern:
 "How do you drill from Region to State in a viz?"

Trap:
 "Add State to Rows manually"

Correct (cleaner):
 Create a hierarchy: Region → State → City
 Drag Region to Rows
 Click + on pill or drill in viz → expands to State
 Same + button to go deeper to City

This is standard Tableau drill-down behavior
Auto-created for date fields: Year → Quarter → Month → Day

Trap 12: Aggregation in scatter plots

Question pattern:
 "You drag two measures (Sales and Profit) to make a scatter, but only one dot appears."

Trap:
 Forgetting that Tableau aggregates measures by default

Correct:
 Analysis menu → uncheck "Aggregate Measures"
 Each row becomes its own dot
 OR: add a dimension to Detail (drills it down)

This is a common practical issue in real Tableau use

Trap 13: Default totals confusion

Question pattern:
 "Grand total shows the SUM of all averages, not the overall average. Why?"

Trap:
 Assuming grand totals re-aggregate measures

Correct:
 By default, totals use the SAME aggregation as the row values
 Sometimes you want a different aggregation for totals
 
 Right-click measure → Total using → Average / Sum / etc.
 Or use Aggregate Using → Server (re-compute at total level)

This catches people on percentage and average totals

Trap 14: Set actions vs filter actions

Question pattern:
 "You want users to click multiple bars to add them to a comparison group."

Trap:
 Filter action — but filter replaces selection, not accumulates

Correct:
 Set action with "Add values to set" behavior
 Each click adds another value to the set
 Set membership drives color/filter in other charts

This is the pattern for "selection stack" interactions
Modern Tableau dashboards use this heavily

Trap 15: Tableau Public vs Desktop

Question pattern:
 "Where should you save a workbook with confidential data?"

Trap:
 Tableau Public (it's free, why not?)

Correct:
 Tableau Public saves to a PUBLIC URL — everyone sees it
 Confidential data must NEVER go to Tableau Public
 Save locally (.twbx) or to Tableau Server / Cloud

Memorize:
 Tableau Desktop (paid): save anywhere (local, server, cloud, public)
 Tableau Public (free): saves only to Tableau Public (publicly visible)

Quick reference card

ScenarioRight answer
Numeric ID treated as measureConvert to Dimension
Date trend over multiple yearsContinuous Date Value
Compare months across yearsDiscrete Date Part
Top N within filterAdd filter to Context
Customer lifetime valueFIXED LOD on Customer
Multi-fact tables, different grainRelationships, not Joins
% of totalSUM(x) / {FIXED : SUM(x)}
Running totalQuick Table Calc
YoY growthQuick Table Calc → YoY
Top 10 dynamic flagSet (Top N condition)
Combine duplicate spellingsGroup
Slow live dashboardSwitch to Extract
Scatter shows one dotDisaggregate Measures
Need user-controlled thresholdParameter + reference line
Confidential dataNOT Tableau Public

Test-day strategy

★ EXAM TIPS
  • Read every word — Tableau wording is precise; one word changes the right answer
  • Eliminate obviously wrong answers first
  • Mark uncertain for review; come back if time permits
  • Don't overthink — first instinct usually right for foundational concepts
  • Watch for "EXCEPT" and "NOT" in question stems
  • Drag-and-drop is unforgiving — verify before submitting each step
  • ~60 seconds per question average; flag long ones
  • Stay calm on tricky questions — pacing matters more than perfection
★ ON THE EXAM

"Numeric ID as dimension?" → Right-click → Convert to Dimension.

"Date trend?" → Continuous Date Value.

"Month comparison across years?" → Discrete Date Part.

"Top N within filter?" → Add filter to Context.

"Customer LTV in viz?" → {FIXED [Customer] : SUM([Sales])}.

"Fan-out from join?" → Use Relationships.

"% of grand total?" → SUM(x) / {FIXED : SUM(x)}.

"Dynamic Top 10 flag?" → Set with Top tab.

"Combine alternate spellings?" → Group.

"Slow live query?" → Switch to Extract.

"Scatter shows one point?" → Disaggregate Measures.

"User-set threshold?" → Parameter + reference line.

"Confidential viz?" → NOT Tableau Public.

"Click to multi-select?" → Set Action.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Numeric IDs (Customer ID, ZIP) need converting to Dimension
  • Date Part vs Date Value: parts are names/numbers (Jan, 1); values are actual dates
  • Discrete blue dates = headers; Continuous green dates = axis
  • Groups combine values into custom categories; Sets mark IN/OUT (often dynamic)
  • Order of Operations: context filters change Top N behavior
  • FIXED ignores viz grain; INCLUDE adds to it; EXCLUDE removes from it
  • FIXED respects only context and source/extract filters by default
  • Relationships solve multi-grain fan-out issues that joins create
  • Live vs Extract: real-time vs performance trade-off
  • Data blending: per-worksheet, LEFT-only, primary determines grain
  • Filters shelf restricts rows; Marks card encodes existing rows
  • Synchronize Axis on dual-axis when scales should be comparable
  • Hierarchies enable + button drill-down (auto-created on dates)
  • Disaggregate Measures via Analysis menu when scatter shows one point
  • Tableau Public is public — never store confidential data
  • Sets enable click-driven selection accumulation via Set Actions

This is a representative mock exam covering the four exam domains. Work through each question, attempt your answer, then read the explanation. Aim for 75% (the passing threshold) before scheduling the real test.

How to use this mock

15 questions across all four exam domains
Multiple choice format (single answer unless noted)

Suggested approach:
 1. Cover the explanation
 2. Pick your answer
 3. Reveal explanation
 4. Note any pattern you missed
 5. Review at the end: which domain did you struggle with?

Time yourself: ~60 seconds per question = ~15 minutes for the full set
The real exam gives you ~80 seconds per question, so this pace is exam-realistic.

Question 1 (Concepts)

Which file format saves a workbook with all data and assets packaged together?

A) .twb
B) .twbx
C) .tds
D) .tdsx
★ ANSWER 1

B) .twbx

The "x" suffix indicates a packaged file. .twbx packages the workbook (.twb) plus any extracts and external files (images, custom shapes). It's self-contained — emailable.

.twb references external data; .tds is a data source only; .tdsx is a packaged data source.

Question 2 (Concepts)

A field appears as a blue pill when dragged to Rows. What does this indicate?

A) The field is a measure
B) The field is continuous
C) The field is discrete
D) The field is a calculated field
★ ANSWER 2

C) The field is discrete

Blue = discrete (creates headers). Green = continuous (creates axis).

Discrete and continuous is independent of dimension vs measure: a measure can be discrete (each value as a header), and a dimension can be continuous (date as an axis).

Question 3 (Preparing Data)

You have monthly sales files named "Sales_2024_01.csv", "Sales_2024_02.csv", etc.
A new file is added each month. What approach automatically includes new files?

A) Manually union files each month
B) Use the Folder connector with a wildcard
C) Append data with Power Query (not Tableau)
D) Re-extract each time
★ ANSWER 3

B) Use the Folder connector with a wildcard

Wildcard union (Sales_2024_*.csv) auto-includes new files matching the pattern at next refresh. The Sheet and Path columns are auto-added to track provenance.

Manual union requires editing each month; the goal is automatic discovery.

Question 4 (Preparing Data)

You connect to a CSV file. Some columns are dates but Tableau detected them as strings.
What's the most efficient fix?

A) Create calculated fields wrapping each in DATE()
B) Click the type icon at the top of each date column and choose Date
C) Re-export the source file with explicit date types
D) Tableau Prep is required for this
★ ANSWER 4

B) Click the type icon at the top of each date column and choose Date

Type icons at column tops in the Data Source preview let you change column types directly. Once changed, date functions (DATEPART, DATEADD) work normally.

Wrapping in DATE() creates extra fields; re-exporting is overkill; Tableau Prep isn't needed for this.

Question 5 (Preparing Data)

Which Tableau feature combines fact tables at different granularities WITHOUT inflating
aggregations through fan-out?

A) Cross-database join
B) Custom SQL
C) Relationships
D) Inner join
★ ANSWER 5

C) Relationships

Relationships (introduced 2020.2) keep tables logically separate and let Tableau query each at the correct granularity per viz. Joins force one physical table — causing fan-out duplication.

Both INNER joins and custom SQL inflate totals when tables have different grains.

Question 6 (Exploring Data)

You have a measure Sales and dimension Region. You drag Sales to Rows.
What aggregation does Tableau apply by default?

A) Average
B) Count
C) Sum
D) Median
★ ANSWER 6

C) Sum

The default aggregation for numeric measures is SUM. Change it via right-click pill → Measure → choose other aggregation, or set a workbook-wide default via right-click field → Default Properties → Aggregation.

Question 7 (Exploring Data)

You drag Order Date to Columns and Sales to Rows. The chart shows three columns
labeled 2022, 2023, 2024 with gaps between them. You want a smooth time axis.
What do you change?

A) Make YEAR(Order Date) continuous
B) Add another dimension to Color
C) Switch Mark type to Bar
D) Add YEAR as a filter
★ ANSWER 7

A) Make YEAR(Order Date) continuous

By default, YEAR is discrete (blue pill, creates headers with gaps). Right-click pill → toggle to Continuous (green pill) → year becomes a smooth axis.

Or right-click pill → choose Year as a Date Value instead of Date Part.

Question 8 (Exploring Data)

A user applies a Top 5 filter on Customer by SUM(Sales) and a Region = "East" filter.
The viz shows only 2 customers when expecting 5. Why?

A) Tableau's Top filter is bugged for "East"
B) The Top 5 applied globally, then Region filter narrowed to East
C) The customers aren't tagged East correctly
D) Need to convert to a Set
★ ANSWER 8

B) The Top 5 applied globally, then Region filter narrowed to East

By Order of Operations, Top N filter applies BEFORE dimension filters. So the global top 5 customers are selected first, then Region narrows — possibly leaving fewer than 5.

Fix: Right-click the Region filter → Add to Context. Context filters run BEFORE Top N, so Top 5 will be computed within East only.

Question 9 (Exploring Data)

You want to show each order along with that customer's total lifetime spend
in a separate column. Which calculation type fits?

A) Aggregate calculation: SUM(Sales)
B) Row-level calculation: Sales
C) FIXED LOD: {FIXED [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])}
D) Table calculation: RUNNING_SUM(SUM(Sales))
★ ANSWER 9

C) FIXED LOD: {FIXED [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])}

The viz grain is order-level (each row is one order). To show the CUSTOMER total, you need a calculation at a different grain. FIXED ignores viz grain and computes per the specified dimension(s).

Result: every order from the same customer gets the same customer-total value displayed.

Question 10 (Exploring Data)

You drag Sales and Profit to Rows to create a scatter plot. Only ONE point appears.
Why, and what's the fix?

A) Data has only one row; check the source
B) Tableau aggregates measures by default; uncheck Analysis → Aggregate Measures
C) Need to drag both measures to Columns instead
D) Scatter plots aren't supported in this view
★ ANSWER 10

B) Tableau aggregates measures by default; uncheck Analysis → Aggregate Measures

By default, Tableau aggregates measures — collapsing all rows into a single (SUM, SUM) point. To see one mark per row, disaggregate via Analysis → uncheck "Aggregate Measures".

Alternative: add a dimension to Detail to disaggregate per dimension value (e.g., per Customer).

Question 11 (Exploring Data)

You need to mark the top 10 customers dynamically (as data changes) so other
vizzes can highlight them. Which feature?

A) Group
B) Set with Top tab
C) Bin
D) Hierarchy
★ ANSWER 11

B) Set with Top tab

Sets mark values as IN or OUT — and can be dynamic (Top tab uses "Top N by measure" and recomputes as data changes). Groups are static manual combines.

Bins discretize a measure; hierarchies are for drill-down.

Question 12 (Sharing)

On a dashboard, you want users to click on a region in a map and have other charts
filter to that region. Which dashboard feature?

A) Highlight action
B) Filter action
C) URL action
D) Parameter action
★ ANSWER 12

B) Filter action

Filter action: clicking marks in one sheet filters target sheets. Configure via Dashboard menu → Actions → Add Action → Filter.

Highlight: emphasizes but doesn't filter. URL: opens webpage. Parameter: updates a parameter value (related but different intent).

Quick alternative: click the sheet on the dashboard → Use as Filter (funnel icon).

Question 13 (Sharing)

You want a layout where four charts are arranged in a 2x2 grid with consistent
sizes that resize together. What's the best approach?

A) Floating objects with manual positioning
B) Two Vertical containers inside a Horizontal container
C) Single tiled drop on the canvas
D) Use a Story with four points
★ ANSWER 13

B) Two Vertical containers inside a Horizontal container

Layout containers ensure children align and resize together. Horizontal at the outer level holds two Vertical containers (left and right columns). Each Vertical container holds the two charts that stack in that column.

Floating objects don't auto-resize; a single tiled drop won't guarantee equal cell sizes; stories are sequential not gridded.

Question 14 (Sharing)

You want to present an analysis as a linear walkthrough with insights captioned at
each step. Which Tableau feature is best?

A) Dashboard
B) Worksheet
C) Story
D) Bookmark
★ ANSWER 14

C) Story

Stories are sequential collections of dashboards/sheets with caption text per point. Perfect for walkthroughs and executive presentations.

Dashboards are for free exploration; worksheets are single charts; bookmarks save a single view state.

Question 15 (Concepts)

Which describes the difference between data blending and a join in Tableau?

A) Blending requires same-server tables; joins don't
B) Joins require same-server tables; blending works across data sources per worksheet
C) They are functionally identical
D) Blending only works with Excel files
★ ANSWER 15

B) Joins require same-server tables; blending works across data sources per worksheet

(Tableau cross-database joins are an exception — they merge tables from different sources into one logical model.)

Blending: per-worksheet, primary + secondary data sources, LEFT-join semantics, secondary aggregates to primary's grain.

Joins: same-source-only physical merge into one table; specific join type chosen.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
